articles.title: Drewry and Cargoo integrate freight benchmarks into procurement platform
articles.summary: Drewry Shipping Consultants has partnered with ocean freight management platform Cargoo to integrate freight benchmarking data into its digital procurement system. The agreement allows customers who use Cargoo and belong to the Drewry Benchmarking Club to access their benchmark data directly within the platform. The...
articles.body: Drewry Shipping Consultants has partnered with ocean freight management platform Cargoo to integrate freight benchmarking data into its digital procurement system. The agreement allows customers who use Cargoo and belong to the Drewry Benchmarking Club to access their benchmark data directly within the platform. The integration connects market rate information with freight procurement, carrier negotiations and contract management. It aims to help shippers compare offers and monitor transportation costs throughout the contract period. However, access is limited to Drewry Benchmarking Club members who are also Cargoo customers. Benchmark data supports freight negotiations Through the integration, eligible shippers can compare carrier quotations with Drewry’s benchmark rates for individual trade lanes. The platform displays both the lowest and average benchmark rates. It also provides access to container shipping forecasts covering seven quarters. These figures can help procurement teams set rate targets before launching tenders. They can then compare incoming offers against market benchmarks during each bidding round. The system also links tender results with carrier contracts and shipment bookings. According to Drewry’s announcement, Cargoo checks bookings against the agreed contract rates. Its freight auditing functions also review invoice charges while disputes can still be raised. This approach allows shippers to use benchmarking information beyond the initial negotiation stage. Tender preparation remains a challenge The partnership comes as shipping companies and cargo owners prepare for upcoming freight contract negotiations. Recent Drewry Benchmarking Club polls show that 44% of participating members need five to seven weeks to prepare a request for quotation (RFQ). Meanwhile, half of respondents reported needing eight to twelve weeks to complete the full bidding process. The surveys also found that one in four members could not identify their annual detention and demurrage expenditure. These findings highlight the difficulties procurement teams face when collecting shipment data, reviewing carrier proposals and tracking freight costs. The integration is designed to address some of these challenges by combining benchmark rates, tender management and shipment execution in one system. Cargoo’s platform connects procurement decisions with capacity allocations, carrier contracts and bookings. It also uses shipment performance and spending data to support future tender planning. Drewry has previously highlighted the importance of stronger contract terms and freight rate benchmarking when negotiating ocean freight agreements. The companies have not disclosed the number of customers using the new integration or any measured cost savings resulting from its introduction.
takeaways: Drewry Shipping Consultants has partnered with ocean freight management platform Cargoo to integrate freight benchmarking data into its digital procurement system.
The agreement allows customers who use Cargoo and belong to the Drewry Benchmarking Club to access their benchmark data directly within the platform.
The integration connects market rate information with freight procurement, carrier negotiations and contract management.

Join the leading maritime news network Photo credit: Shutterstock/Igor Grochev OSLO, Nov 10 (Reuters) – President Donald Trump’s energy chief said on Tuesday the US was confident that the first cargo of Russian diesel headed for the US would eventually get sold in the global market despite the tanker carrying it coming to a halt recently. Shipping data showed on Tuesday that the Agioi Fanendes has come to a halt off the US east coast. The haltfollowed warnings by a US governor and lawmakers about the legality of the ship’s landing in the US. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, asked whether he was concerned that the vessel, which had originally signaled it was headed to New York, had been turned away, said he had no worries. “Not at all. No, it’ll go to another port,” Wright told reporters in New Orleans. “We just want that diesel going into the world markets.” President Donald Trump last month announced a surprise deal with Moscow to import diesel from Russia to help lower prices at the pumps ahead of this month’s US midterm elections. New Jersey’s Democratic Governor Mikie Sherrill this month warned local port officials and terminal operators against accepting Russian diesel, saying those shipments would break federal law. Sherrill said importing Russian diesel could expose businesses and individuals using New Jersey ports to harsh civil and criminal penalties. Senators from both parties said last month that US law bars imports of energy from Russia until it ends aggression against Ukraine. The Malta-flagged tanker was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulfur diesel in Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, LSEG shipping data showed, with an expected delivery date of November 7. But Eastmed, the Greece-based company which manages the tanker, said a week later that the vessel was proceeding awaiting orders and that a port of discharge had not yet been nominated or finalized. “Nothing has changed regarding the vessel’s destination, she is still awaiting orders,” Greece-based vessel manager Eastmed told Reuters on Tuesday. Vessels may change their declared destination or revert to “for orders” status more than once during a voyage when a prospective deal falls through, plans change or the operator does not wish to declare its intended destination. Other tankers carrying Russian diesel which had signaled the US Atlantic Coast as their destination later altered course, shipping data showed. Former President Joe Biden had imposed a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Trump in approving the deal last month waived parts of a new US sanctions law on Moscow and said Russia would immediately export 300,000 tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Ellie Valencia, a senior analyst at Vortexa, said the ship’s speed had come down from 10 knots several days ago to about 2 knots currently. “What you can interpret from the speed is directly related to the status of the ship which is “FOR ORDERS,” most likely meaning that it doesn’t yet have a specific buyer,” Valencia said. articles.title: Mitsui E&S raises profit outlook as port equipment earnings improve
articles.summary: Mitsui E&S has raised its full-year earnings forecast following stronger performance in its logistics systems and industrial businesses during the first half of fiscal 2026. The Japanese engineering group reported net sales of ¥175 billion ($1.15 billion) for the six months ended 30 September 2026, an increase of...
articles.body: Mitsui E&S has raised its full-year earnings forecast following stronger performance in its logistics systems and industrial businesses during the first half of fiscal 2026. The Japanese engineering group reported net sales of ¥175 billion ($1.15 billion) for the six months ended 30 September 2026, an increase of 5.7% year on year. Operating income rose 4.8% to ¥20.7 billion, while new orders increased 8.2% to approximately ¥158 billion. However, profit attributable to owners of the parent company edged down 0.6% to ¥17.4 billion. The company now expects full-year operating income of ¥40 billion, up from its previous forecast of ¥34 billion. Its revenue outlook remains unchanged at ¥370 billion for the fiscal year ending 31 March 2027. Port equipment business records higher earnings Mitsui E&S reported improved results in its Logistics Systems division, which supplies container cranes and related services. Segment revenue increased 7.1% to ¥33.3 billion, supported by progress on major construction projects in Japan and overseas. Operating income climbed 15.8% to ¥7.8 billion, reflecting higher sales and improved project profitability. However, new orders declined 39.9% to ¥19.7 billion. The company attributed the decrease mainly to large contracts secured in Southeast Asia and the United States during the corresponding period last year. Despite the decline, Mitsui E&S reported continued demand for container handling equipment. The company is also expanding its international business, including in Latin America, where it secured an order for environmentally friendly rubber-tyred gantry cranes in Argentina. Meanwhile, the group continues to develop remotely operated and automated cranes as part of its wider efforts to expand its port equipment portfolio. Marine engine orders rise despite earnings pressure The Marine Propulsion Systems division recorded a 29.3% increase in new orders to ¥81.2 billion. Higher demand for marine engines, including dual-fuel models, supported the growth. Nevertheless, segment revenue fell 3.2% to ¥72.7 billion, while operating income declined 37.8% to ¥5.6 billion. Mitsui E&S attributed the weaker earnings to lower sales and higher-than-expected costs associated with developing and introducing new products. The company continues to expand its alternative-fuel engine portfolio, including LNG, LPG, methanol and ammonia technologies. Looking ahead, Mitsui E&S raised its forecast for annual operating income in Logistics Systems from ¥10 billion to ¥15 billion. However, it lowered the corresponding forecast for Marine Propulsion Systems from ¥12 billion to ¥11 billion. The group also increased its projected annual dividend from ¥60 to ¥65 per share. The latest forecast revision follows an earlier upgrade announced after the company’s first-quarter results . Mitsui E&S expects continued demand for marine propulsion systems and port equipment, although development costs and the timing of project deliveries remain important factors for profitability.

articles.summary: Russian crude exports on G7 tankers fell sharply in October as Greek operators were enticed by strong earnings elsewhere and steered away from Black Sea conflicts, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) and Maritime Intelligence Risk Suite data. The data shows tankers flagged, owned or...
articles.body: Russian crude exports fall on G7 tankers as Greek operators flee for better earnings in International Shipping News 11/11/2026 Russian crude exports on G7 tankers fell sharply in October as Greek operators were enticed by strong earnings elsewhere and steered away from Black Sea conflicts, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) and Maritime Intelligence Risk Suite data. The data shows tankers flagged, owned or operated by companies based in G7 countries and their allies, or insured by Western protection and indemnity clubs, loaded roughly 906,000 barrels per day of Russian crude in October, or 24.2% of total exports. The share was the lowest in seven months. In September, G7 tankers lifted 1.2 million b/d, or 29.2% of total exports. Shipments by tanker operators in Greece, the top shipowning nation within G7/EU, more than halved to 8.3 million barrels in October from 17.3 million barrels in September, according to CAS/MIRS. October’s loadings were the lowest since December 2024. The development came as tanker rates were around their all-time highs in mainstream markets, boosted by larger ship requirements from offshore transfers east of the Strait of Hormuz and high risk premiums during the ongoing US-Iran war. October’s average Suezmax time-charter-equivalent earnings for transporting Russian crude from the Baltic to West Coast India was $46,257.92 per day lower than the Global Suezmax Index, compared with a discount of $23,225.69/day in September, according to Platts assessments for non-scrubber, non-eco ships. Platts is part of S&P Global Energy. In a research note published last month, CAS analysts said four Greek-owned Aframaxes and four Suezmaxes had migrated from Russian to mainstream trades where earnings environments were strong. Greek tanker firms have also been avoiding operations in the Black Sea, with the CAS/MIRS data showing only one Greek-operated tanker lifting Russian crude in the region last month, compared with 11 in other regions. The International Maritime Organization said more than 100 ships might have been hit in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov this year as part of the Russia-Ukraine war, potentially killing 38 seafarers. Platts assessed the additional war risk premium for crude exports from the Black Sea at $5/b on Nov. 6, the highest since the assessment began in October 2022. Shadow fleet The non-G7 fleet, mainly composed of shadow tankers amassed by Russia and opaque owners to bypass Western sanctions, lifted 2.8 million b/d of Russian crude in October, according to CAS/MIRS. This compared with 2.9 million b/d in September. Tankers operated by Hong Kong firms were responsible for shipments of 27.7 million barrels last month, Russian companies for 22.5 million barrels, and UAE companies for 15.6 million barrels. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright last month said his country planned to allow legitimate businesses to acquire sanctioned tankers for non-sanctioned trades to reduce shipping costs in mainstream trades, though Washington has yet to announce a detailed relief proposal. A total of 42 tankers have migrated from potentially illicit trades in Russia, Venezuela and Iran to mainstream markets so far this year, according to the CAS note, though none of them have been formally sanctioned by the US. “Migrated vessels were rapidly absorbed into mainstream Middle East Gulf export chains following their transition into compliant employment,” CAS analysts said, adding that a growing proportion of operators have opted to remain in compliant markets once migration occurs. In September, G7 tankers lifted 1.2 million b/d, or 29.2% of total exports.

articles.title: Shipping in New Crossroads After the US Mid-Term Election
articles.summary: The shipping market is facing renewed uncertainty after the latest developments in the US and the mid term elections’ results. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Xclusiv said that “the November 3rd US midterm elections reshaped Washington’s political landscape, with Democrats securing both the House and Senate,...
articles.body: Shipping in New Crossroads After the US Mid-Term Election in Hellenic Shipping News 11/11/2026 T he shipping market is facing renewed uncertainty after the latest developments in the US and the mid term elections’ results. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Xclusiv said that “the November 3rd US midterm elections reshaped Washington’s political landscape, with Democrats securing both the House and Senate, delivering a significant setback to President Trump. Inflation, elevated energy prices and the prolonged conflict with Iran weighed heavily on voters. Although the new Congress takes office in January 2027, the outcome could increase pressure for adjustments in US foreign, energy and trade policies, with potentially significant implications for global shipping. Oil markets responded sharply. On November 4th, Brent declined 8.7% to USD 94.62/barrel, while WTI fell 8.3% to USD 88.12/barrel, reflecting expectations of a possible de-escalation with Iran. By November 6th, Brent was heading towards a weekly decline of approximately 16%, potentially its steepest since 2020. Nevertheless, continued attacks on vessels in the Persian Gulf demonstrate that diplomatic expectations do not necessarily translate into immediate improvements in maritime security or energy supplies”. Source: Xclusiv shipbroker According to Xclusiv, “for tanker markets, the implications are particularly interesting and potentially contradictory. A gradual restoration of Middle Eastern exports could increase crude shipments, supporting VLCC and Suezmax employment. Equally important is the potential restocking of commercial and strategic petroleum reserves following months of disruptions. Replenishing inventories could temporarily generate substantial additional cargo volumes, supporting tanker utilisation and freight rates. However, more oil moving does not necessarily mean greater tanker demand. Normalisation through Hormuz and potentially the Red Sea could shorten trading distances, while reduced congestion, waiting times and diversions would release previously constrained tonnage. This improvement in fleet productivity effectively increases available vessel supply without additional newbuilding deliveries. Consequently, an initial freight recovery driven by restocking and cargo availability could eventually face downward pressure as tonne-mile demand and vessel utilisation adjust”. The shipbroker added that “Russia introduces another important variable. October’s Washington–Moscow agreement facilitating Russian diesel exports, accompanied by partial sanctions waivers, demonstrated Trump’s prioritisation of energy affordability, although actual US deliveries remain uncertain. Democratic control of Congress could encourage tougher sanctions and stronger support for Ukraine. Renewed restrictions might extend trading distances and reinforce shadow fleet activity, while diplomatic progress and sanctions relief could gradually restore Russian cargoes to mainstream tanker markets, potentially reducing tonne-mile demand”. Meanwhile, “shipbuilding policy also faces uncertainty. Washington’s ambition to strengthen domestic shipyards and challenge Chinese dominance retains bipartisan appeal, although implementation costs and effectiveness may face greater scrutiny. The proposed extension of the Section 301 suspension until January 9th, 2027, could provide temporary relief for Chinese-built tonnage. Nevertheless, uncertainty over future port charges could influence chartering flexibility, vessel liquidity, secondhand values and newbuilding preferences. Meanwhile, a Democratic Congress may challenge additional tariffs, although presidential executive authority limits immediate policy reversals. Any easing of US-China trade tensions could support containerised and dry bulk trade, while persistent restrictions would continue reshaping sourcing patterns and trading distances”, Xclusiv said. “From an S&P perspective, owners and investors must distinguish temporary geopolitical freight premiums from sustainable earnings. Strong spot markets do not automatically justify elevated asset values when normalisation could rapidly increase effective fleet availability. Ultimately, the elections introduce competing forces rather than a straightforward bullish or bearish outlook. For shipping, the decisive factor is not simply whether geopolitical tensions ease, but how cargo volumes, trading distances and available fleet capacity respond”, the shipbroker concluded. Nikos Roussanoglou, Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide Tops 2026-11-11 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Atlantic Tanker Earnings Fall Faster Than Gulf Earnings
articles.summary: The TD3C/TD22 earnings ratio rose from 2.73 on 30 October to 3.10 on 6 November, as US Gulf–China VLCC earnings fell 16.2% to around $415,000/day, against a 4.8% decline on Middle East Gulf–China to $1.29 million/day. All 16 dirty tanker benchmarks fell over the week, with the steepest declines in the Atlantic and...
articles.body: Atlantic Tanker Earnings Fall Faster Than Gulf Earnings in International Shipping News 11/11/2026 T he TD3C/TD22 earnings ratio rose from 2.73 on 30 October to 3.10 on 6 November, as US Gulf–China VLCC earnings fell 16.2% to around $415,000/day, against a 4.8% decline on Middle East Gulf–China to $1.29 million/day. All 16 dirty tanker benchmarks fell over the week, with the steepest declines in the Atlantic and Mediterranean. Several Suezmax and Aframax routes lost 50% or more of their earnings, while Middle East Gulf VLCC losses remained below 5%. Both TD3C (Middle East Gulf–China) and TD22 (US Gulf–China) reached their October earnings peaks on 8 October, although the subsequent correction has been considerably sharper on the Atlantic route. By 6 November, TD22 earnings had fallen 34.9% from their October high, compared with a 9.0% decline on TD3C. The sharper fall in Atlantic earnings pushed the TD3C/TD22 ratio to 3.10 at the end of the week, its highest level since 18 September and above its 12-month average of 2.77. Freight: Atlantic Crude Routes Lead the Decline The ten largest percentage declines in the dirty basket were all on routes loading West of Suez, as classified in Chart 2 and the table below. Suezmax West Africa–UK Continent (TD20) fell 46.6%, Guyana–ARA (TD27) 52.6%, and Black Sea–Mediterranean (TD6) 37.2%, while MEG–Mediterranean (TD23) fell 8.4% and remained 3.2 times TD20. Among Aframaxes, Cross-Mediterranean (TD19) fell 69.8% and US Gulf–ARA (TD25) fell 60.8%, against 3.8% on Kuwait–Singapore (TD8). All 16 routes remain above their year-earlier and three-month reference levels. Supply: Westbound Ballasters Rise as the Fleet Stays East Signal Maritime recorded 49 active westbound VLCC ballasters on 8 November, compared with 45 a week earlier. Of these, 43 originated in the Far East. Brazil was the leading destination with 18 vessels, followed by South Africa with 10 and the African Atlantic Coast with eight. The count remains below the late-October peak of 52, and monthly East-to-West ballast movements fell from 73 in September to 50 in October. Westbound positioning rose faster in the smaller crude segments. Suezmax ballasters increased to 51 from 45 a week earlier, with 24 heading for the Africa Atlantic Coast. Aframax ballasters rose to 60 on 7 November from 45 on 31 October, with 28 heading for the US Gulf. Arrival dates, onward employment and regional cargo demand will determine how much of this tonnage becomes available for fixing. The increase in westbound ballasters contrasts with the continued concentration of VLCC tonnage east of Suez. The East/West fleet ratio stood at 5.11 on 7 November, close to its 2026 high of 5.18, compared with 3.75 in 2025 and 3.27 in 2024. Regionally, VLCC positions increased by 13.0% around Africa and 9.2% in Europe, while the Americas recorded a 12.3% decline. The Middle East Gulf count was broadly unchanged at 189 vessels. These figures capture the geographical distribution of VLCCs across all employment states, rather than the number of vessels immediately available for new employment. Flows and Transport Costs Signal Ocean tracked crude flows from all origins averaged 45.7 million b/d in October, down 6.6% year on year but well above May’s low. Tracked flows attributed to Saudi Arabia averaged 2.32 million b/d, down 66.3% year on year and below every earlier month of 2026. These are tracked and attributed flows, not a definitive measure of physical Saudi crude exports: the comparison does not establish how much of the decline reflects lower physical exports or changes in the attribution of ship-to-ship cargoes. OPEC estimates that Middle East–East Asia VLCC freight rose from $3.18/bbl in the week of 26 January to $37.13/bbl in the week of 26 October, and insurance from $0.06/bbl to $12.29/bbl. On OPEC’s basis, freight and insurance combined accounted for about 30% of the total delivered cost of a barrel of crude on this route, against about 5% in January. These are OPEC estimates of the cost borne by cargo, not tanker TCE earnings. Hormuz Freight Watch: Macro Risks Conditions around the Strait of Hormuz remained uncertain in early November. Diplomatic contacts continued without a confirmed agreement, and security incidents involving commercial vessels were reported in and around the strait during the week. For shipping, the practical effects are on owners’ willingness to accept Gulf employment, war-risk insurance terms and voyage times, none of which can be assumed to normalise on a fixed timetable. Oil prices fell sharply after the US midterm elections amid hopes of de-escalation, while TD22 declined 16.3% between 3 and 6 November; the freight data do not isolate the effect of the election from other market changes. Transport costs remain elevated, with freight and insurance at about 30% of total delivered cost on Middle East–East Asia VLCC voyages on OPEC’s estimates. Seven OPEC+ producers maintained their December production targets on 1 November, leaving planned supply levels unchanged ahead of their next meeting on 29 November. Potential changes to tanker availability and export capacity remain unconfirmed: the approval process outlined on 19 October for acquiring and refurbishing sanctioned tankers has yet to result in confirmed additions to mainstream chartering capacity, while comments attributed to Saudi Arabia’s energy minister on 12 October indicated that converting a gas pipeline could add about 1.2 million b/d of crude capacity towards the Red Sea within seven to eight weeks; completion has not been confirmed, and Yanbu loading capacity remains a constraint. Market Takeaways The tanker freight outlook remains difficult to assess, with geopolitical developments continuing to influence market expectations and vessel employment. Fresh reports of a possible agreement concerning the Strait of Hormuz on 9 November have renewed attention on the prospects for de-escalation, although no agreement or corresponding improvement in shipping conditions has been confirmed. In the Atlantic, the timing of ballast arrivals and fresh cargo enquiry will be important in determining the supply balance for upcoming loadings. The Middle East Gulf presents a different picture, where security concerns, insurance costs and owners’ willingness to trade continue to influence vessel availability. An increase in vessel transits would not, on its own, establish that normal chartering conditions have been restored. With these differences persisting, the timing and scale of any freight adjustment remain uncertain. Source: By Maria Bertzeletou, Signal Ocean Group Tops 2026-11-11 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: COP31: Broad maritime coalition launches breakthrough 20% electrification goal by 2035
articles.summary: This decade is critical for decarbonizing the maritime sector. Integrated energy planning, accelerated action and ambitious policy implementation are vital to keep international shipping on track for net-zero by or around 2050. Whilst the maritime sector is not yet a major consumer of electricity, there are many...
articles.body: COP31: Broad maritime coalition launches breakthrough 20% electrification goal by 2035 in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 11/11/2026 T his decade is critical for decarbonizing the maritime sector. Integrated energy planning, accelerated action and ambitious policy implementation are vital to keep international shipping on track for net-zero by or around 2050. Whilst the maritime sector is not yet a major consumer of electricity, there are many cost-effective opportunities to increase its use. Delivering maritime electrification will require coordinated action across vessels, ports and terminals, landside freight, utilities and grids, renewable generation and, increasingly, renewable fuel production. Ports sit at the intersection of these systems and will be critical energy and implementation nodes for the transition. COP31 presents an electrification goal: raising the share of global final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035 (up from just over 20%), cutting fossil fuel dependence, and driving sector transitions. Many international and regional initiatives, coalitions and alliances already promote maritime decarbonization. This Maritime Electrification Breakthrough Goal aims to align political and collective action to accelerate the deployment and expansion of electrification. Our Shared Goal We, representing the maritime sector from across the value chain, support the COP31 Maritime Electrification goal by aligning our actions with the following target: ● Increase electricity’s share of shipping’s final energy demand to at least 20% (additional 2EJ) by 2035. Our Commitments In pursuit of these goals, and according to our respective roles, authorities and capabilities, we commit to: ● Share knowledge and lessons learned, publishing reports and key findings to accelerate the deployment and reduce learning costs. ● Participate in public/private platforms, initiatives, pilot projects, and demonstrations that help advance technical readiness, global standardization and policies that incentivize electrification in every region. ● Ensure a just transition by supporting the development of a skilled workforce both on the ship and port side supporting current workers at risk of displacement from the energy transition doing so in an equitable and inclusive manner. ● Work with finance institutions to increase and facilitate access to capital for large-scale electrification infrastructure projects in ports and shipping. ● Review progress annually until 2035 including by improving data collection to establish baselines and track global progress towards these goals. We intend to work collaboratively and expeditiously towards this goal. We are confident that these collaborative actions will deliver lasting benefits for the maritime sector, port communities, emerging economies and the global climate. Our Call to Governments We urge Member States to adopt a progressive set of climate measures at the IMO in 2026 that support the realization of the 2023 GHG Strategy, measures that can also provide a clear signal to unlock the sector’s urgent electrification investments. In addition, we call on Member States to integrate measures related to maritime electrification in their NDCs, and support the integration of this topic in the Second Global Stocktake. Current energy demand and the electrification pathway For shipping’s direct energy use, the final energy demand is estimated at around 10EJ. Domestic and short-sea shipping outside the international-shipping boundary, port and terminal operations, and port-related landside transport represent additional maritime-related energy demand but are not included in the quantified 20% target. Electricity used upstream to produce renewable fuels is likewise not counted as final energy demand electrification. These activities are nevertheless critical to the broader maritime energy transition and to the infrastructure, markets and energy systems needed to deliver the goal. Total demand is expected to stay approximately constant or rise slightly, taking into account growth in trade, transport demand and also efficiency. The large majority of shipping’s energy use is currently met through the use of fossil fuels consumed in internal combustion engines. Within this broader system, direct electricity use is expected to grow through several interconnected pathways: ● Deployment of Onshore Power Supply (OPS) in ports; currently deployed in about 3% of cruise ship terminals, plus container and bulk terminals in the USA, China and Europe. ● Share of fleet powered by battery electrification: More than 1,600 battery-powered vessels are in operation globally, including fully electric and hybrid ships. Significant potential remains for cost-effective expansion, particularly on shorter international voyages, although deployment continues to face challenges related to charging infrastructure, maintenance and local capacity. ● Electrification of landside port operations; an estimated 100,000–120,000 container handling equipment units need to be decarbonized as well as port and port-related land-transport (trains, road vehicles, harbour craft). Some terminals are already electrified; for example, APM Terminals Suape is Latin America’s first 100% electrified container terminal. These pathways are interconnected. As maritime electricity demand grows, ports will increasingly function as energy and implementation nodes connecting vessels and terminals with landside freight, utilities and grids, renewable generation and, in some locations, renewable fuel production. Coordinated planning across these systems can aggregate demand, improve infrastructure utilization, support investment in grid capacity and renewable generation, and reduce the risk of fragmented or stranded infrastructure. Whilst the maritime sector is not yet a major consumer of electricity, there are many cost-effective opportunities to increase its use.

Delivering maritime electrification will require coordinated action across vessels, ports and terminals, landside freight, utilities and grids, renewable generation and, increasingly, renewable fuel production.

articles.title: Carriers may secure only part of their November rate increases as Suez returns, Sogese report says
articles.summary: Freight rates to Europe have rebounded since early October after falling steadily from their July peak, but the conditions behind the rebound are mixed. Cargo demand is positive, with Far East to Europe volumes up 12.2% in the first seven months of the year, according to Xeneta. Ships, however, are arriving late, and...
articles.body: Carriers may secure only part of their November rate increases as Suez returns, Sogese report says in International Shipping News 11/11/2026 Freight rates to Europe have rebounded since early October after falling steadily from their July peak, but the conditions behind the rebound are mixed. Cargo demand is positive, with Far East to Europe volumes up 12.2% in the first seven months of the year, according to Xeneta. Ships, however, are arriving late, and the return of Suez routings is releasing capacity faster than schedules are recovering. In its November Europe Container Market Update, Sogese reads this as a market moving from a disruption premium to a capacity-management test, in which the price carriers announce and the price shippers actually pay are drifting apart. For Italian importers and exporters, the cost of delay and of choosing the wrong route can matter more than the headline ocean rate. How Sogese reads the market 1. Carriers are testing prices, and November is the test Drewry’s World Container Index reached $4,585 per 40ft on 22 October, its highest in 15 weeks, and had fallen to $4,389 by 5 November, 4.3% below the peak. MSC filed FAKs of $4,500 to North Europe and $5,000 to the West Mediterranean and Adriatic for 1 to 14 November, and CMA CGM filed $4,900 for the West Mediterranean. Drewry’s assessments for Shanghai to Rotterdam ($3,615) and Shanghai to Genoa ($4,166) sit below those levels, and Drewry counted five announced Asia-Europe blank sailings for the following week, which it read as ample capacity that makes the increases uncertain. A FAK is a carrier’s request. Until announced increases appear in what customers actually pay, Sogese treats the rebound as unconfirmed. “October is the point where the market begins to separate geopolitical risk from capacity reality. If Suez keeps normalising, the key question for 2027 will not be whether there are enough ships, but how aggressively carriers manage the capacity that comes back into the market.”Andrea Monti, CEO & MD, Sogese 2. Suez is releasing hidden capacity before reliability recovers The same fleet has alternated between scarcity and abundance in 2026. The Hormuz crisis that began in February removed usable capacity and raised costs. The return to Suez now puts capacity back. BIMCO, citing Clarksons Research, puts weekly container capacity through the Suez Canal at 753,000 TEU in the first two weeks of October, against 1,457,000 TEU in the same weeks of 2023. Alphaliner counted 63% of Far East to Europe capacity on loops using Suez in at least one direction on 21 October. Premier Alliance has shortened the scheduled round trip on FE1 from 13 to 11 weeks and on IOX/INX from 13 to 10 weeks, with first westbound Suez transits scheduled for 9 and 17 November. What carriers do with the released tonnage decides the market effect. Weekly departures with fewer ships mean fleet efficiency. Added sailings or capacity reach rates and space. Hormuz remains the main risk to this picture, since an escalation could offset much of the capacity Suez returns. “My base case is that Suez will be the majority route for Asia-Europe by year-end, but I do not expect a clean, irreversible industry-wide return by 31 December. Full commercial normalisation – reliable schedules, stable insurance and confidence that services will not switch back – is more likely to extend into Q1 2027, potentially early Q2.”Andrea Monti, CEO & MD, Sogese 3. Delay is the larger cost Only 4% of Far East to Europe arrivals were on time in September, with an average delay of 9.9 days, according to Xeneta. Globally, 27% of arrivals were on time, with an average delay of 6.0 days. A delay of that size weighs on stock, production and customer commitments more than a difference of a few hundred dollars per container, and a shorter Suez transit does not remove it. Vessel bunching during the transition can add congestion at terminals even when demand is stable. 4. Italian gateways are diverging Shanghai to Genoa gained 12.7% between 8 October and 5 November, against 8.3% for Rotterdam, and the Genoa premium over Rotterdam widened from $359 to $551 per 40ft. Inland links add to the difference. Trieste handled 528,125 TEU from January to September, up 2.5%, with the third quarter up 22.3%, yet its train movements fell 14.0% to 5,206 because of European corridor restrictions. Contship Italia puts the average rail share at La Spezia Container Terminal at 33% and aims for 50% once its Ravano expansion is complete. Italian companies also face cost pressure beyond freight: ISTAT reports consumer inflation of 4.2% in September and industrial producer prices up 13.8% on the year. The effective cost of a gateway depends on the onward connection and on energy and inventory costs as well as the ocean rate. What stakeholders should act on between now and spring 2027 Sogese expects controlled normalisation as its base case, with a renewed security shock as the main alternative. The advice below is built to hold under both. For its November outlook the report also sets out three paths: partial uptake of announced increases, failure of the increases to reach market rates, and uneven capacity and pricing as Suez rotations are rebuilt. Importers and shippers • Now to mid-December: negotiate on the executable quote. Compare surcharge treatment, validity and confirmed space on a named sailing, and re-quote weekly while FAKs remain in play. Treat Drewry’s 12 and 19 November releases and the expiry of the 1 to 14 November FAKs as the first evidence of what the market will pay. • Through the first quarter of 2027, during the contract season: budget in scenarios and name the trigger that moves the business from one case to another. Protect the volumes that cannot fail, and keep a meaningful share flexible or indexed. As an illustration, a protected core of 60 to 80% with the remainder indexed or flexible, calibrated by lane and risk tolerance. • In the contract itself: state the expected routing (Suez or Cape), the transit-time range, the notice period and the re-pricing trigger if the route changes. Separate BAF, war-risk and emergency charges, tie them to named indices or caps, and agree removal triggers. Define the on-time measure, rollover and blank-sailing protection, and allocation fulfilment. • From spring: monitor delivery after award, including allocation, blanks, rollovers, on-time performance and actual all-in cost. If Suez normalisation proceeds, negotiating leverage on Asia-Europe improves, and Sogese advises spending part of it on service quality and flexibility, not only on the lowest rate. “For 2027 I would avoid making one rate bet. Protect the core volumes that cannot fail, keep a meaningful share flexible or indexed, and negotiate routing and surcharge clauses as carefully as the base freight rate. The goal is not to predict every shock; it is to make the contract survive one.” Andrea Monti, CEO & MD, Sogese Exporters The Drewry lanes in this report run from Asia to Europe and do not price Italian exports. ISTAT reports that Italy’s extra-EU exports grew 5.8% from January to September, and Hapag-Lloyd says its Italian export volumes have grown more than 20% since 2021 and that it will keep expanding in northern Italy and strengthen its presence in the south and the Adriatic. • Now to mid-December: confirm space, cut-offs and connections on each sailing, and agree a fallback departure before committing delivery dates to customers. • Through the first quarter of 2027: use the broader carrier presence in Italian regions to test alternatives, and watch ISTAT’s October release on 27 November for the direction of extra-EU trade. Forwarders and logistics operators • Now to mid-December: show customers the full cost of a route, including gateway, carrier, onward train or truck and expected delay, rather than the ocean rate alone. • Through the first quarter of 2027: pre-qualify alternative Italian and Northern Range gateways and rail connections for critical flows before disruption, not after the primary route fails, and align ocean schedule changes with inland slots. Container owners, lessors and traders Faster Suez rotations improve box velocity. If the same cargo needs fewer boxes in circulation, a shortage can turn into a regional surplus faster than cargo demand changes. Over the next six months, lease duration, off-hire terms and repositioning rights matter more than chasing the highest current daily rate, and early depot returns in Europe and the Mediterranean are the first warning sign. “I would be cautious about buying or leasing equipment purely because today’s network feels tight. If Suez becomes the dominant Asia-Europe route during Q1 2027, container velocity improves immediately. A box shortage can turn into a regional surplus faster than underlying cargo demand changes.” Andrea Monti, CEO & MD, Sogese Terminals and inland operators Gateways differ in how much cargo leaves by rail, and the Trieste and La Spezia figures show the spread. Over the next six months the practical task is to keep inland capacity matched to ocean schedules that are changing as rotations are rebuilt. What would change the picture Sogese will track these signals: Suez’s share of Asia-Europe capacity sustaining above roughly 60 to 70% with two-way use; Hormuz incident frequency; Drewry’s index and blank sailing count on 12 and 19 November; what MSC and CMA CGM do when their FAKs expire after 14 November; the first Premier Alliance transits; schedule reliability against 4% on the Far East to Europe trade; European depot returns; and ISTAT’s October extra-EU trade release on 27 November. Source: Sogese 2026-11-11 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Cargo demand is positive, with Far East to Europe volumes up 12.2% in the first seven months of the year, according to Xeneta.
Ships, however, are arriving late, and the return of Suez routings is releasing capacity faster than schedules are recovering.
For Italian importers and exporters, the cost of delay and of choosing the wrong route can matter more than the headline ocean rate.

articles.title: Marine biodiesel demand to more than double by 2031 without IMO framework – IEA
articles.summary: Global marine biodiesel demand will rise from just under 1 billion litres/year (around 890,000 mt/year) in 2025 to nearly 2 billion litres/year (around 1.78 million mt/year) by 2031, the International Energy Agency (IEA) forecasts. That estimate assumes the IMO does not adopt its Net-Zero Framework, the global rules...
articles.body: Marine biodiesel demand to more than double by 2031 without IMO framework – IEA in International Shipping News 11/11/2026 Global marine biodiesel demand will rise from just under 1 billion litres/year (around 890,000 mt/year) in 2025 to nearly 2 billion litres/year (around 1.78 million mt/year) by 2031, the International Energy Agency (IEA) forecasts. That estimate assumes the IMO does not adopt its Net-Zero Framework, the global rules it has approved to cut GHG emissions from shipping. Even so, marine biodiesel would make up only 0.6% of total marine fuel use by 2031, the IEA says. It will remain the main source of renewable energy in shipping, but it will account for just 1% of the growth in renewable energy use across all transport. Europe, where the FuelEU Maritime regulation is in place, will drive four-fifths of the growth. The IEA expects marine biodiesel to deliver much of the region’s near-term emission cuts while alternative fuels and energy efficiency measures are scaled up. Most of the remaining increase will come from Singapore and China, where ports fuel vessels trading to Europe. Growth elsewhere will stay limited because of weak policy support. FuelEU Maritime took effect at the start of 2025. It requires ships above 5,000 GT calling at EU ports to cut the GHG intensity of the energy they use. GHG intensity is measured well-to-wake and counts emissions from producing and distributing a fuel as well as burning it. The required cut is 6% by 2030 and 14.5% by 2035. It covers all energy used on voyages within the EU and half of the energy used on voyages into or out of the bloc. IMO framework would accelerate demand The report says demand will climb much higher if the IMO adopts its Net-Zero Framework. In that case, the IEA sees marine biodiesel use rising to more than 12 billion litres/year (more than 10.68 million mt/year) by 2031, or 4% of total marine fuel demand. A vote on the framework was pushed back from 2025 and is now due in December. The framework would cover roughly 97% of the world’s merchant fleet by tonnage and set two tiers of targets for cutting the GHG intensity of ships’ fuel. By 2030, ships would pay $100/mtCO2e for emissions above the tougher target of a 21% cut, rising to $380/mtCO2e for emissions above the base target of an 8% cut. The IEA expects most ships to meet the 8% target by blending lower-emission fuels or buying credits, with marine biodiesel, liquefied natural gas (LNG) and liquefied biomethane (LBM) among the cheaper options available. The 21% target would be harder to reach, as bio-methanol, e-methanol and ammonia remain scarce and costly, and the penalty for missing it is much lower, the report says. The IEA assumes marine biodiesel supply would be enough for most ships to hit 8%, but not 21%, with competing road transport demand limiting supply. Asia Pacific would take the biggest share of that extra demand. Its marine biodiesel use would reach around 6 billion litres/year (around 5.34 million mt/year) by 2031 in this scenario, roughly double Europe’s, according to IEA data. Source: By Nachiket Tekawade, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news/ 2026-11-11 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Xeneta Ocean Outlook 2027: Three Years, Three Shocks, And What Comes Next
articles.summary: For the third year running, 2026 began with an expectation that ocean container rates would soften. For the third year running, a shock got there first. In 2024 it was the rate spike impact of Red Sea conflict escalation. In 2025 it was US tariffs. In 2026 it was conflict in the Middle East and ...
articles.body: Xeneta Ocean Outlook 2027: Three Years, Three Shocks, And What Comes Next in International Shipping News 11/11/2026 For the third year running, 2026 began with an expectation that ocean container rates would soften. For the third year running, a shock got there first. In 2024 it was the rate spike impact of Red Sea conflict escalation. In 2025 it was US tariffs. In 2026 it was conflict in the Middle East and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Major supply chain shocks have been a fact of life in ocean container shipping in the post-Covid-19 era. The numbers tell the story. Spot rates from the Far East to the US West Coast are up 343% in October compared with 28 February, the day before the Middle East crisis began. That is just 14% short of the all-time high set in 2022 during the pandemic era spike. Every major fronthaul out of the Far East, to North Europe, the Mediterranean and the US East Coast, has seen triple-digit spot rate increases during 2026. Shippers did not only pay more in the wake of the Middle East crisis. They waited longer, or did not receive their cargo at all. Global on-time arrivals fell to 27% in Q3 2026, with the average delayed container arriving six days late. So what does 2027 look like? The Xeneta Ocean Outlook 2027 forecasts global average spot rates to fall 30% and long-term contract rates to fall 5% across the full year, measured against a Q3 2026 baseline. The fundamentals point down. The question is whether something else gets in the way again. The case for softening rates in 2027 A forecast for softer rates rests on supply outrunning demand. Xeneta expects the global container fleet to grow 6.8% in 2027, with 2.9m TEU of new capacity arriving against 0.5m TEU scrapped. Demand will grow 2.5% to 4%. That gap is wide enough to loosen the market on its own. The demand number needs context. Volumes grew 4.7% in the first eight months of 2026, but much of that was frontloading. Shippers pulled cargo forward to beat fuel surcharges and the risk of further disruption. Far East to US volumes rose 11% in August while inflation-adjusted US retail sales grew 1.9%. That gap will close. Expect a slow start to 2027 as summer inventories are drawn down, followed by a weaker peak season. Supply gets a second boost from the Red Sea. Weekly capacity crossing the Red Sea reached 467,297 TEU in October, half the level seen before the crisis began in 2023. Shorter Suez loops need fewer ships, and 599,000 TEU of nominal capacity has already been released back into the global fleet in 2026. More will follow in the first half of 2027 as carriers convert one-way strings into full loops. One structural shift works in carriers’ favour. Growth is concentrated on fronthaul trades, where a container earns far more than on the return leg. Fronthaul volumes are up 37% on 2019 while backhaul volumes are down 8%. China now exports six containers for every laden container it imports, up from 3.3 in 2019. This imbalance absorbs capacity and will hold up rates on the busiest lanes even as the global average falls. The risks that override the fundamentals Xeneta has named “the unknown” as a key risk in every Ocean Outlook since 2024. Each year it arrived. A forecast built on supply and demand is the right starting point, but recent history shows how quickly a single event overpowers it. The known risks for 2027 start with fuel. Singapore high sulphur bunker prices are up 107% since 27 February. Carriers passed that on, and the average fuel surcharge on long-term contracts across the four major Far East trades rose 42% to USD 820 per FEU. If fuel prices ease in 2027, shippers need to check that surcharges fall with them. The Gulf remains closed to most container traffic. Before the conflict, 99 services called at Arabian Gulf ports. Jebel Ali went from 423,000 TEU of weekly arrivals to 9,000. Even if the Strait of Hormuz reopens, carriers will keep their footholds in Jeddah, Khor Fakkan and Sohar rather than return in full. Tariffs have gone quiet without going away. US imports from China are down 9% on 2024 while imports from South East Asia are up 31%. Shippers moved their sourcing rather than cutting volumes, and sector-specific tariffs will keep them on alert through 2027. Then there is the Panama Canal. El Niño puts water levels back on watch for the dry season at the start of 2027. Some carriers are already charging Panama surcharges despite minimal restrictions. Reliability will improve, but check what sits behind the number Global on-time arrivals ended Q3 2026 at 27%, with Far East to Europe falling to 4% in September after four typhoons closed Chinese ports in quick succession. Xeneta expects a rebound in the first half of 2027 as new ships arrive and demand softens, but with a ceiling of around 40%. The quality of that rebound matters as much as its size. Carriers can lift on-time percentages by blanking sailings or padding published transit times. In Q2 2026, China to US West Coast sailings arrived almost four days ahead of schedule. A better on-time number achieved through fewer sailings is not a more reliable service. Gemini Cooperation will keep its reliability lead in 2027, but by a narrower margin. Its on-time rate fell from 70% in June to 40% in September, and it now sits 4 percentage points ahead of non-alliance services. A premium that has fallen this far will be harder to defend in 2027 tenders. What this means for your freight A 30% fall in the global spot average is not a 30% fall on your lanes. The right forecast for your business depends on which corridors you ship, whether you sit on a fronthaul or a backhaul, how exposed you are to Gulf routing, and how your contracts handle fuel surcharges and routing changes. The six themes in the full report, from fleet composition by trade lane to carrier-level reliability, were written to answer those questions, and they land differently for every shipper. The analysts behind the Outlook, including myself, Emily Stausbøll and Destine Ozuygur, have one piece of advice for 2027: use data and intelligence to assess risk continuously, in calm periods and in crises. Market intelligence means you negotiate from a stronger position and understand the context you are operating in. This article is the short version. The full Ocean Outlook 2027 (available in IQ Hub for Xeneta customers) covers six themes in depth, with lane-by-lane rate forecasts, fleet and capacity analysis by trade, chokepoint scenarios and carrier-level reliability data. It is not published openly. Our commercial team walks shippers through it one to one, mapping the forecasts against your trade lanes, your contracts and your 2027 tender timeline. For the third year running, a shock got there first.
In 2024 it was the rate spike impact of Red Sea conflict escalation.

articles.title: Korea shipbuilders face LNG carrier price squeeze as North America orders seen next year
articles.summary: Some in the shipbuilding industry are voicing worries that the liquefied natural gas (LNG) carrier market has peaked and is set to cool. Freight rates for LNG carriers are falling, and new order prices are coming down amid competition with China. LNG carriers are the flagship high-margin vessel type where Korean...
articles.body: Korea shipbuilders face LNG carrier price squeeze as North America orders seen next year in Shipbuilding News 11/11/2026 Some in the shipbuilding industry are voicing worries that the liquefied natural gas (LNG) carrier market has peaked and is set to cool. Freight rates for LNG carriers are falling, and new order prices are coming down amid competition with China. LNG carriers are the flagship high-margin vessel type where Korean shipbuilders have shown strength. Others say the boom in the LNG carrier market is not over yet. Korean shipbuilders are counting on orders from LNG liquefaction projects in North America. They expect related orders to kick into gear in the United States and Canada starting next year. Pushed into low-priced orders amid competition with China According to the shipbuilding industry and Clarksons Research on the 10th, 76 large LNG carriers of 174,000-cubic-meter class (cargo tank capacity) or bigger were ordered from January through October this year. By country, Korea won 44 ships (57.9%) and China won 32 (42.1%). This year’s LNG carrier orders roughly doubled from a year earlier, but demand has shown signs of slowing in the second half. Large LNG carrier orders totaled 59 ships in the first half but came to 17 through October in the second half. LNG carrier freight rates have also fallen sharply from the start of the year. As of early this month, rates for 174,000-cubic-meter LNG carriers were down about 23% on the Atlantic route and about 40% on the Pacific route compared with early this year. Shipbuilders are also watching the downtrend in the ship new building price for LNG carriers. According to Clarksons Research, the ship new building price for a 174,000-cubic-meter LNG carrier fell from an average of $248 million in January this year to $245 million in October. In fact, contract prices for newbuild LNG carriers at Samsung Heavy Industries, which has the most LNG carrier orders among Korean shipbuilders, have dropped from late last year and early this year. Samsung Heavy Industries won two 174,000-cubic-meter LNG carriers for 743 billion won ($251.38 million per ship) in December last year, but the most recent order, for two ships on the 2nd of last month, was priced at 672.2 billion won ($247.20 million per ship). At its third-quarter earnings briefing on the 29th of last month, Samsung Heavy Industries acknowledged it had recently taken LNG carrier orders at low prices. LNG carriers are Samsung Heavy Industries’ core vessel segment. The company has won orders for 20 LNG carriers this year. Some analysts say China’s rising share of LNG carrier orders is pressuring Korean shipbuilders to lower prices. China’s orders for large LNG carriers fell from 28 ships in 2024 to five in 2025 due to the end of Qatar’s ordering cycle, then rebounded this year. In China, latecomers are entering the LNG carrier market after leaders Hudong–Zhonghua Shipbuilding and Jiangnan Shipyard. With Hengli Heavy Industry, a fast-growing player based in Dalian, Liaoning Province in the northeast, joining in, the number of Chinese shipyards building large LNG carriers has risen to six. Samsung Heavy Industries cited Hengli Heavy Industry as a threatening rival, while HD Hyundai Heavy Industries pointed to Hudong–Zhonghua Shipbuilding and Jiangnan Shipyard. On the decline in Korea’s market share and prices due to China’s rising LNG carrier orders, Samsung Heavy Industries said it is “carefully monitoring developments in China.” Bae Gi-yeon, an analyst at Meritz Securities, said, “Capacity expansion and new entrants at Chinese shipyards are putting downward pressure on the ship new building price for LNG carriers,” adding, “The pricing competitiveness of low-cost LNG carriers from Chinese shipyards is bound to stand out.” The broader base of Chinese yards is forcing Korean shipbuilders to cut prices to win orders. Orders expected next year for North American LNG projects Even so, inside and outside the shipbuilding industry, some expect LNG carrier demand will not drop off sharply. GTT of France, which owns the core technology for LNG cargo tanks, recently said it sees no signs of a slowdown in LNG carrier demand. According to GTT’s third-quarter results released on the 23rd of last month, the company booked 80 orders in the first to third quarters this year, nearly triple the 27 in the same period last year. Of those, 71 were for LNG carriers. Because the LNG cargo tank is the key system that stores LNG, GTT’s design contract tally is viewed as a major indicator of the LNG carrier market. According to GTT, LNG liquefaction projects worldwide that reached a final investment decision (FID) from last year through the third quarter of this year have combined capacity of 135 MTPA (million tonnes per annum, 135 million tons a year). GTT said most of the LNG carriers needed for these projects have not yet been ordered. The shipbuilding industry estimates around 200 LNG carriers will be required. GTT CEO Francois Michel said at the earnings briefing, “Orders will be placed soon,” and, “We have no information or discussions that would lead us to think demand is slowing.” LNG liquefaction and export projects in North America are seen as the biggest swing factor for future LNG carrier demand. Notable projects include Commonwealth LNG in Louisiana, Delfin LNG in the Gulf of Mexico, and LNG Canada Phase 2 in British Columbia, Canada. In July, GTT forecast an additional 550 LNG carriers would be ordered over the next 10 years through 2035. That was an increase of about 100 from its previous outlook of more than 450. With investment in LNG liquefaction projects speeding up, centered on North America, it expects demand for LNG carriers to rise. Vessels that need to be in service in 2030 are expected to start being ordered from next year. A HD Hyundai Heavy Industries official said, “Buyers see the current ship new building price as the bottom and are coming to the table,” adding, “This is not a situation to worry about.” Jang Seong-ho, an analyst at IBK Securities, said, “With capacity expansions at LNG liquefaction plants centered on the United States, the LNG carrier order market is expected to be strong next year.” Source: ChosunBiz 2026-11-11 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Freight rates for LNG carriers are falling, and new order prices are coming down amid competition with China.
LNG carriers are the flagship high-margin vessel type where Korean shipbuilders have shown strength.
Others say the boom in the LNG carrier market is not over yet.

articles.title: USCG Warns Shipowners to Verify Air Draft, Avoid Bridge Strike
articles.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) has issued a Marine Safety Alert warning vessel owners, operators and crews to verify their ships' maximum air draft before transiting beneath bridges and other overhead obstructions, following an incident in which…
articles.body: USCG Warns Shipowners to Verify Air Draft, Avoid Bridge Strike Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 10, 2026 copyright karegg/AdobeStock The U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) has issued a Marine Safety Alert warning vessel owners, operators and crews to verify their ships' maximum air draft before transiting beneath bridges and other overhead obstructions, following an incident in which an unaccounted-for antenna struck a bridge. In Safety Alert 17-26, issued November 10, 2026, the Coast Guard detailed its investigation of a deep-draft vessel that contacted a bridge despite voyage-planning calculations indicating sufficient vertical clearance. Investigators determined that the vessel's reported air draft was based on outdated plans that did not reflect its current configuration. Multiple versions of the ship's plans were maintained on board, and the documents used to calculate air draft failed to account for an installed MF/HF tiltable antenna extending above the vessel's reported highest point. Because the antenna was omitted from the calculation, the crew did not recognize the need to lower it before passing beneath the bridge. The vessel's pilot subsequently received an understated air-draft figure, creating a false margin of safety during transit planning. The incident highlights the risks associated with vessel modifications and equipment installations that alter a ship's vertical profile without corresponding updates to technical documentation and operating procedures. The Coast Guard recommends that shipowners and operators incorporate air-draft verification into their safety management systems, maintain current vessel-specific drawings, and clearly identify or remove superseded documentation. Operators should also establish procedures for configuring movable equipment before overhead-clearance transits and require positive confirmation that antennas and other adjustable structures are properly lowered or secured. The alert was developed by USCG Sector Los Angeles–Long Beach and distributed by the Coast Guard's Office of Investigations and Casualty Analysis.

articles.body: Valenciaport and Shanghai International Port Group held a joint presentation for their clients at the Shanghai Tower, aimed at showing the business opportunities between the two ports and strengthening cooperation on green corridors. The event was chaired by Mar Chao, President of Valenciaport, and Sam Liu, Vice President of SIPG, and was joined by Guoqiang Shi, CEO of CSP Spain. China is Valenciaport’s largest international market for container traffic. Between January and September 2026, 714,691 TEUs were handled in trade with China, up 15.07% on the same period last year, while cargo tonnage reached 7.66 million tonnes, up 15.75%. The Port of Shanghai accounts for 36 percent of Valenciaport’s trade with China, equal to 2.3 million tonnes a year. Chao described Valenciaport’s position in the Western Mediterranean as making it one of the main gateways for goods moving between Asia, Spain and the rest of Europe, with more than 100 regular shipping services linking it to all five continents. The visit aimed to give Chinese companies first-hand knowledge of what Valenciaport offers as an entry point to the Spanish and European markets, including strong maritime connectivity, rail links to major logistics and industrial hubs, and a hinterland covering a large share of Spain’s economy. Valenciaport handles more than 40% of Spain’s total import and export traffic. She called the port a reliable and competitive partner for Chinese companies’ international growth, and said there is great potential for further collaboration. Digitalisation, innovation and sustainability are the three areas where the Port Authority wants to deepen cooperation with China, since ports will increasingly compete on efficiency, connectivity and the ability to build smarter, more sustainable logistics chains. Valenciaport has long been digitalising its operations and advancing its energy transition. Its Net Zero Emissions Plan targets net zero by the middle of the next decade, with electrification, renewable energy and shore power for vessels already under way. Chao also attended the China International Import Expo in Shanghai, where she met representatives of the Chinese logistics, port and business communities to strengthen Valenciaport’s visibility and positioning in the region.

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Port of Long Beach The Trump administration has formally extended its suspension of port fees targeting Chinese-built and Chinese-operated vessels for another two months, keeping the controversial measures on hold while Washington continues trade negotiations with Beijing. The decision, published Tuesday in the Federal Register, extends the suspension through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on January 9, 2027, with the measures potentially resuming January 10 unless further action is taken. The extension took effect November 9, preventing the fees from returning following the expiration of an earlier one-year suspension agreed to under a trade deal between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in November 2025. Under the notice issued by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR), shipping companies will not accrue liability for or be required to pay the maritime transport fees established under the administration’s Section 301 investigation into China’s dominance of the maritime, logistics, and shipbuilding sectors. The extension also maintains the suspension of additional duties on Chinese ship-to-shore cranes and other cargo-handling equipment. The measures were originally adopted in April 2025 and subsequently modified in October 2025 as part of a broader effort to counter China’s growing influence over global shipbuilding and maritime transportation. The administration initially suspended the measures for one year beginning November 10, 2025, following a trade agreement between Trump and Xi. The latest extension provides another two months for negotiations. USTR said the circumstances that justified the original suspension remain in place, with discussions between the two countries continuing. The decision follows an October 26 proposal to extend the suspension, which drew approximately 60 unique public comments. According to USTR, supporters argued that keeping the measures on hold would prevent higher shipping costs, avoid commercial disruptions and provide additional time for negotiations with China. Opponents, however, warned that suspending the fees would weaken incentives to invest in American shipbuilding and related industries, potentially allowing China’s dominance of the sector to grow. Other commenters urged the administration to permanently eliminate certain maritime service fees, citing potential disruptions to U.S. exports. Some also called for the tariffs on Chinese cargo-handling equipment to be considered separately from the vessel fees. Despite the extension, USTR emphasized that rebuilding American shipbuilding capacity remains a priority. During the suspension, the administration said it would continue working to expand domestic commercial shipbuilding, develop a more resilient maritime workforce and coordinate with allies to strengthen U.S. shipbuilding capabilities. The extension also leaves open the possibility that the fees could return early next year. USTR said it will continue monitoring China’s maritime and shipbuilding practices and consider whether to extend the suspension again or take further action before the January 10 deadline. The decision comes as China has also extended its suspension of retaliatory port fees targeting U.S.-linked vessels until January 10, 2027, according to a Reuters report on Monday. China also extended its suspension of an investigation into the security of shipping and shipbuilding supply chains. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Port of Brunswick The Georgia Ports Authority is expanding automotive shipping capacity at the Port of Brunswick as a growing number of global automakers establish manufacturing operations across the state, strengthening Georgia’s position as a major hub for vehicle production and logistics. At its annual State of the Port of Brunswick event on Tuesday, port officials highlighted new automotive investments, rising demand for roll-on/roll-off (RoRo) shipping and a nearly $5 billion infrastructure investment program planned over the next decade. The Port of Brunswick, which the authority identifies as a U.S. leader in automotive imports and exports, has experienced 277% growth over the past decade, according to the authority. Its three RoRo berths at Colonel’s Island handled 50 vessels in October alone. A fourth RoRo berth is now 60% complete and scheduled to open in December 2027. The expansion will increase capacity and accommodate newer generations of vehicle carriers capable of transporting more than 10,800 car equivalent units (CEUs). The additional berth is expected to improve vessel turnaround times while providing room for future growth in vehicle imports and exports. “Georgia Ports are creating opportunities for businesses to grow, enhancing long-term supply chain competitiveness on a state, regional, national and global level, generating new job growth in the port region and throughout the state,” said Georgia Ports Authority CEO Griff Lynch. The expansion comes as Georgia attracts billions of dollars in automotive manufacturing investment. Hyundai Motor Group’s 3,000-acre Metaplant near Savannah is expected to create 8,500 jobs by 2031 and has attracted 22 nearby suppliers. Kia has operated its manufacturing plant in West Point since 2009, while electric vehicle maker Rivian is developing a $5 billion manufacturing facility at Stanton Springs North, expected to create 7,500 long-term jobs by 2030. More recently, Audi announced plans to establish its first U.S. manufacturing plant near Macon, Georgia. The German automaker intends to invest $4 billion in the facility, creating approximately 4,500 jobs. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2027, with production expected in the early 2030s. Other major automakers, including BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Volvo, already use Brunswick for finished-vehicle shipments and processing. Georgia Ports Authority President Kevin Price said the state’s expanding automotive manufacturing base is also supporting growth in other cargo segments. “The automotive manufacturing ecosystem continues to grow here. We’re also seeing strong growth in the heavy machinery market such as construction equipment and farm equipment,” Price said. While Brunswick handles finished vehicles and heavy equipment, the Port of Savannah serves as a major gateway for containerized automotive parts and components. According to the authority, Savannah handles approximately 40 vessel calls per week, 15,000 daily truck gate transactions and 42 double-stack trains weekly through its Mason Mega Rail facility, connecting the port to inland markets via Norfolk Southern and CSX. The Georgia Ports Authority’s nearly $5 billion investment plan includes five additional container ship berths in Savannah and the fourth RoRo berth in Brunswick. Over the past decade, the authority’s board has approved $4.13 billion in infrastructure improvements. The investments are intended to position Georgia’s ports for continued growth in automotive manufacturing, vehicle exports and imports, and containerized trade as manufacturers expand their U.S. operations.
