articles.title: MSM: Shipmanagement’s next advantage will be trust not size
articles.summary: Consolidation is reshaping shipmanagement, but Faouzi Fradi, chief executive of MSM, does not believe getting bigger has to mean becoming more distant from owners, vessels or seafarers. MSM, formerly known as Maryam Shipmanagement, recently rebranded as part of a broader shift from a predominantly group-focused...
articles.body: Maritime CEO Middle East Operations MSM: Shipmanagement’s next advantage will be trust not size Splash November 11, 2026 0 190 5 minutes read MSM MSM Consolidation is reshaping shipmanagement, but Faouzi Fradi, chief executive of MSM, does not believe getting bigger has to mean becoming more distant from owners, vessels or seafarers. MSM, formerly known as Maryam Shipmanagement, recently rebranded as part of a broader shift from a predominantly group-focused shipmanager towards an international third-party management platform, while also moving into new headquarters in Dubai. “The rebrand is only the starting point. It signals our transition from being mainly a group-focused shipmanager into a broader international third-party management platform.” Over the next three to five years, Fradi expects MSM to grow selectively in technical and crew management, backed by stronger procurement, performance and commercial-administration capabilities. Dubai will remain its centre, while the company strengthens its reach through Turkey, Greece, Norway, India and the Philippines. “We are not pursuing fleet growth or geographical expansion for its own sake. We want controlled growth, closer access to clients, and owners who value transparency, direct access to decision-makers and a manager prepared to think like an owner.” MSM is positioning itself as an owner-aligned alternative to the largest global shipmanagement groups. Fradi acknowledges the advantages that scale can bring, particularly in systems and purchasing power, but argues that size can also create drawbacks. “Large managers bring scale, systems and purchasing power, and these are real advantages. But scale can also create layers, slower decisions and additional costs.” He sees accessibility, flexibility, cost discipline and direct accountability as areas where a smaller manager can compete while still maintaining strong systems and compliance. At MSM, senior management remains close to the vessels and resources can be moved according to operational need. During a dry docking or serious technical problem, Fradi says the vessel may have the CEO, technical manager, procurement manager and several superintendents directly involved. “We work collaboratively and make decisions quickly. That combination of quality, responsiveness and value-for-money is where a boutique manager can genuinely compete.” The challenge is retaining that approach as the company grows. “We need sufficient scale to attract good people, negotiate effectively with suppliers, invest in technology and maintain specialist capability. But scale should strengthen a shipmanager, not create distance between the owner, the management team and the vessel.” MSM intends to maintain relatively focused and accountable operating teams while supporting them with common systems, standards, procurement capabilities and governance across the company. For Fradi, there is no target fleet size that defines success. “For me, the objective is not to reach a particular fleet number. It is to build an organisation that can grow substantially without becoming bureaucratic or losing direct access to senior management. If we can achieve that, then growth becomes an advantage rather than a compromise.” Dry bulk and tankers offer the most immediate opportunities because MSM already has the people, systems and operating experience in those sectors. Its team also has experience with containerships and offshore vessels. Specialised segments require greater preparation. “For specialised sectors such as LNG, LPG or VLCCs, technical knowledge alone is not enough; the crewing pool and competence base must also be built carefully. We would be happy to develop those capabilities with owners who share that long-term approach. Growth should follow capability, not the other way around.” Fradi also sees opportunities with owners that initially outsource selected functions before moving towards full management. Dubai forms an important part of the growth strategy. Fradi points to its proximity to owners, charterers, financiers, traders and service companies, along with its position between Europe and Asia. “It is also an attractive base for international talent, with strong infrastructure, safety, financial services and global air connections. Traditional European and Asian centres remain extremely important, but Dubai offers a combination of access, speed and resilience that is difficult to replicate.” He expects meaningful growth from Middle Eastern owners, although MSM’s ambitions remain global. “Our task is to show clients elsewhere that a Dubai-based manager is not more distant; with modern communications and international offices, it can be closer, faster and highly competitive.” Technology is another part of the expansion. MSM is investing in AI-assisted reporting, predictive maintenance, fleet performance tools and AI-assisted charterparty administration. Fradi sets a straightforward test for whether the technology is worthwhile. “The test for AI is simple: does it save time, improve a decision or prevent cost? If not, it is simply another technology layer.” MSM uses AI-assisted tools to structure reporting, identify exceptions in fleet data, support maintenance prioritisation and organise charterparty obligations, deadlines and claims. Fradi says the company has also seen value in complex project tracking, including dry docking, where AI-assisted job and expense monitoring has improved visibility and decision speed. “AI will not replace the superintendent or manage a seafarer’s career. Its role is to reduce administrative workload and give experienced people more time for judgement.” The same emphasis on practical decision-making shapes MSM’s approach to decarbonisation. Fradi does not believe a responsible shipmanager can currently tell owners that there is one obvious fuel solution for the 2030s. “The sensible approach is to preserve optionality.” That starts with measures that already create value, including hull and machinery efficiency, voyage optimisation, accurate data, maintenance discipline and retrofits with a clear payback. Fuel choices then need to be assessed against trading pattern, vessel age, charter profile, remaining economic life, infrastructure availability and carbon exposure. Crew competence presents another long-term challenge. Fradi expects the greatest pressure to emerge among experienced senior officers and engineers, particularly those familiar with automation, electronic engines, alternative fuels and increasingly digital ships. “The shortage is not only about numbers; it is about competence.” Managers, he argues, need to recruit earlier, continuously develop people and create clearer career paths between sea and shore. Pay remains important, but predictable rotations, connectivity, shore support and respect for leave increasingly influence retention. Training, in particular, cannot be treated purely as a certification requirement. “It has to be continuous and aligned with the technology, fuels and operating environment seafarers are expected to manage.” At the same time, geopolitics, sanctions and changing trade patterns are making vessel operations more complicated and expensive. Fradi points to the need for greater due diligence around sanctions regimes, banking restrictions and counterparties, while war zones and high-risk areas are adding to crewing costs and operational complexity. “Owners can underestimate how quickly these risks interact: crew may be unwilling to transit a high-risk area, tensions can escalate rapidly, and procurement or spares logistics can be disrupted at the same time.” That makes liquidity and rapid decision-making at vessel level increasingly important. Looking five years ahead, Fradi expects successful managers still to need strong systems, commercial discipline, cost control, good people and the right technology. But he does not see any of those as the ultimate differentiator. “But I believe the real difference will remain something much more human: trust.” For owners, that means knowing the manager will be available and accountable when something goes wrong. “What he wants to know is that when something goes wrong, there is someone on the other side who understands the problem, answers the phone, takes responsibility and genuinely cares about protecting the asset and controlling the cost.” Fradi applies the same principle to seafarers and shore staff, who he says do not want to become employee numbers in a large organisation. Scale and technology can improve shipmanagement, he argues, but neither should create distance. “For me, the successful shipmanager of the future will be the one who can grow without losing the human relationship; with the owner, with the vessel and, most importantly, with the people who make the whole operation possible.” Tags United Arab Emirates Splash November 11, 2026 0 190 5 minutes read Follow Us Facebook X LinkedIn Tumblr Pinterest Reddit VKontakte Messenger Messenger WhatsApp Telegram Share via Email Print

articles.title: ‘Nonsense Rate’: Iran War Exposes Turmoil Behind Key Tanker Benchmark
articles.summary: In March this year, inside a 282-year-old institution responsible for one of the most important prices in global oil markets, one man staged a quiet protest.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche By Jack Farchy and Alex Longley (Bloomberg) — In March this year, inside a 282-year-old institution responsible for one of the most important prices in global oil markets, one man staged a quiet protest. “Nonsense rate,” Christopher Loveday wrote on March 23 in an internal document at the Baltic Exchange, where he was responsible for helping produce the world’s benchmark rate for shipping oil. “Still a nonsense,” he wrote two days later. On March 31, as he filled in his section of the spreadsheet that sets the price of a benchmark underpinning billions of dollars in freight derivatives trading, he wrote: “b/s rate.” The comments are among numerous internal communications, emails and calls that have become public in filings and court testimony during a legal battle playing out in London between the Baltic and oil trader Mercuria Energy Group. Collectively, they offer unprecedented insight into how the war in Iran played out inside a key corner of the global oil market. In particular, the case has provided a fly-on-the-wall perspective on events inside the Baltic, which for centuries has been at the heart of the global shipping industry. It has shown that numerous people involved in the key oil tanker rate, called TD3C, expressed reservations as the Baltic Exchange continued to publish the price in the early weeks of the war. It has put a spotlight on the Baltic’s guidance allowing for derivatives contracts underpinned by TD3C to be used in setting the benchmark itself, which was met with shocked derision by some of the industry’s biggest players. And it has shown tensions running high within the Baltic’s senior staff, with one describing the company as “so rotten.” It’s unclear how the revelations, while embarrassing for the Baltic and its owner Singapore Exchange Ltd., will affect the outcome of the case. Lawyers for the two sides are due to make their closing arguments in court this week, after which the judge could take several months to come to a decision. Mercuria, whose demands have changed several times since it launched the case in April, is seeking to have the judge declare that the Baltic was wrong to keep publishing the TD3C index in the initial phase of the war from March to July. “This is obviously a difficult moment for the Baltic, and it’s important for the market that it comes through this and learns whatever it needs to learn,” said Halvor Ellefsen, a London-based director at Fearnleys Shipbrokers UK Ltd. “Any commodity market needs reliable benchmarks and freight is integral to that.” The Baltic has argued its decision was justified and that, in any case, any breaches of its obligations should be addressed by its regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, rather than in private legal action. It declined to comment for this story while the trial continues. Not an Exchange The Baltic Exchange’s history dates back to 1744, when it was formally established in Threadneedle Street as the Virginia and Baltick Coffee House as a venue for trading commodities — key among them tallow from the Baltic Sea region. While a key cog in global shipping and commodity markets, the institution employed just over 30 people last year and made a pre-tax profit of £379,000, according to its most recent annual accounts. Its offices are in the heart of the City of London, a short walk from the Tower of London. And despite its name, the Baltic Exchange today is not actually an exchange at all: its main role is to collect assessments from a small group of brokers to produce benchmark indexes for the price of shipping. When the US and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, Loveday’s role was to oversee that process for the Baltic’s most important tanker index: TD3C, which represents the cost of hiring a very large crude carrier, or VLCC, on the route from Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia to Ningbo in China. Every day, he would review the numbers submitted by the nine broker “panelists” responsible for assessing the TD3C rate, question any that seemed out of whack to him, and also insert his own estimate of the rate into the Baltic’s spreadsheet — to serve as a sense-checking reference point for comparing the brokers’ numbers. The TD3C index is published just after 4 p.m. every day, using an average of the panelists’ assessments. The crucial question for the Baltic staff in the first days of the war was whether TD3C should be suspended. Over three weeks of hearings, Mercuria’s legal team has argued that the Baltic got the answer wrong. At 9:15 a.m. on the morning of March 2, the first working day after the war began, the Baltic’s small team held a call, according to Loveday’s witness statement. Several of their key routes, including TD3C, involved transiting the Strait of Hormuz — something ships had abruptly stopped doing over the weekend. At that point it was unclear how long the war would last, or whether it would have a lasting impact on the flow of oil. Over the following week, the Baltic had numerous interactions with brokers, traders and shipowners. Tanker traffic through the Strait had all but ceased, and several traders argued that the TD3C rates should be suspended (though Mercuria was not among them — it advocated instead for basing TD3C on alternative routes that were still operating normally). Draft Notice Mark Jackson, a shipping industry veteran who had been CEO of the Baltic since 2017, even commissioned a draft notice announcing the suspension of all rates on routes involving the Strait of Hormuz, he said in his witness statement. Still, there were hopes that the war may end quickly, and when the Baltic held a call for its panelist brokers on March 4, the conclusion was that they were willing to keep submitting assessments. TD3C would continue. Yet Loveday, the Baltic employee most directly responsible for the TD3C process, stopped inputting his own estimates into the Baltic’s spreadsheet. In fact, it was only after the Baltic received a complaint and its head of compliance started looking into TD3C, that Loveday’s boss noticed the missing numbers and told him to restart, according to witness statements from the Baltic executives. Loveday, who worked as a shipbroker for about 28 years before joining the Baltic in 2019, registered his protest in the notes of the spreadsheet. “I don’t see how we can possibly report here,” he wrote on March 20. (He later explained in his witness statement that this had been written while he was waiting for a flight at Houston airport and was “feeling a little ‘non-compliant’.”) He continued to insert snide comments until early April, when a colleague took over as the assessor of TD3C. In his witness statement, Loveday said that his comments were specifically about the futility of his own attempts to estimate the rate, rather than about the benchmark itself. Still, he also said in court that he had thought since the start of the war that TD3C should have been suspended. And Loveday was not the only person involved in the production of TD3C to express concerns. One Baltic staffer said in early April that the rate was “starting to lose credibility”; another told colleagues that if he was not at the Baltic he would have “zero confidence” in the rate, according to transcripts of internal calls cited by Mercuria’s lawyers. When the Baltic convened the panelists on March 16, several argued in favor of a suspension. “It’s purely hypothetical…I think it’s just complete nonsense, the whole thing,” one said. One panelist refused to submit assessments for several weeks, while two other panelists submitted the same value every day for weeks at a time. Still, the Baltic continued to publish the index. It has argued that it was led by the panelists – the brokers with the most information about what tanker deals were being discussed – and that at no point did a majority of them say they couldn’t assess the rate. ‘Extraordinary Circumstances’ Besides continuing to publish TD3C itself, one of the more controversial decisions to emerge from the court proceedings was a piece of guidance issued by the Baltic Exchange, to help the broker panelists to arrive at their assessments of the market. In “extraordinary circumstances,” the Baltic wrote in early March, panelists could base their judgment of the tanker market by looking at price levels in the shipping derivatives contracts – known as forward freight agreements – that were themselves underpinned by TD3C. The inclusion of the reference to the FFA market received an immediate backlash. TD3C was supposed to be based on actual deals being done and discussed in the real world. If TD3C could be set based on movements in the derivatives market, the whole system risked losing touch with reality. “You are literally leaving your index open for direct abuse,” one trader wrote to the Baltic of the decision. “It’s like having a criminal write his own sentence.” When one panelist wrote in the Baltic’s spreadsheet of assessments that they had used the FFA market as a guide, Baltic CEO Jackson told a colleague they should be careful that information “doesn’t get out.” (Jackson said in court that he had simply wanted to avoid further discussions on the subject, though he agreed with Mercuria’s barrister that the comment didn’t reflect the Baltic’s motto “Our Word Our Bond.”) The Baltic has defended its instructions to panelists that they can use the FFA market as a reference point – and indeed the guidance still stands, one of the Baltic’s senior assessors confirmed to the court. In court filings, expert witnesses from the two sides said that physical and FFA markets may inform one another, but noted that FFA information “should not be used as the sole determinant of a physical TD3C assessment.” Freight Surge | Daily earnings for supertankers jumped because of Iran war The significance of the huge derivatives market underpinned by TD3C — worth 17.4 billion euros ($19.4 billion) in the first six months of this year — was highlighted in court for both the Baltic and Mercuria. Mercuria was the largest user of TD3C derivatives, accounting for between 25% and 50% of total open interest, according to its freight derivatives trader David Schickler. It was generally short TD3C derivatives as a hedge for the earnings of its fleet of oil tankers around the world. When the TD3C rates soared at the start of the war, Mercuria’s derivatives positions faced hefty losses. But the company’s tankers didn’t experience a similar surge in earnings, and its traders testified that they weren’t able to sail through Hormuz to take advantage of the high rates supposedly on offer. Mercuria has said its losses as a result of the mismatch were likely to be in the hundreds of millions of dollars, although it has removed that claim from its most recent legal filings. When the Baltic’s lawyer asked Renaud Hauspy, a freight trader at Mercuria, if the effect of Mercuria’s index-linked position had been a “disaster,” Hauspy replied: “It has not been positive.” Mercuria’s lawyers, meanwhile, argued that the size of the FFA market was part of the reason that it kept publishing the benchmark. In a mid-April call, Matthew Cox, the Baltic’s head of benchmark production, asked: “Would we have suspended TD3 had it not been for the open interest, had it not been for the FFAs? And I think had it, you know, had TD3 been a, any other index, we would, we would have, um, suspended.” (Cox told the court that he was incorrect to suggest that every other criterion for suspension had been met.) As the weeks dragged on, frustrations continued to grow inside the Baltic. In one internal call that was read out in court by a lawyer for Mercuria, one of the Baltic’s assessors described the company as “so rotten at the moment.” Since the Baltic’s head of compliance started her job in April 2022, she has received four formal complaints: all of them since the Iran war began, and all of them about TD3C, she said in her witness statement. The most recent of them, on August 12, was from Mercuria itself. Mercuria initially sought in its lawsuit to have TD3C retroactively suspended, but has adjusted its claim multiple times, most recently seeking only that the court rule the Baltic should have suspended the route from March until July. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has picked up sharply during the second half of the year despite the ongoing conflict, with exports from countries other than Iran recently nearing prewar levels. But the trade has remained shrouded in secrecy. And it has increasingly become dominated by one company: Sinokor, which accounted for more than 50% of all transits since early July along the “southern” route by the Omani coast, according to a report produced for the case by maritime security company Ambrey. It’s far from clear that the difficulties assessing tanker rates have gone away. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. REUTERS/Steve Nesius/File Photo The U.S. Department of Energy has closed a $480 million loan to modernize 22 offshore platforms in the Gulf of Mexico, marking the department’s first completed loan financing domestic oil and natural gas production. The financing, announced Tuesday, will support Arena Energy’s Project Elkhorn, a major infrastructure redevelopment effort in the Southern Eugene Island area off Louisiana. The project is expected to increase offshore production by as much as 38,600 barrels of oil and 77 million cubic feet of natural gas per day at peak output. The loan comes through the Department of Energy’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF), formerly known as the Loan Programs Office, which the Trump administration has redirected toward expanding domestic energy production and strengthening existing infrastructure. The Energy Department said the financing was made possible by provisions in President Donald Trump’s Working Families Tax Cut legislation. Arena Energy’s wholly owned subsidiary, Elkhorn Offshore, will use the financing to refurbish and reactivate idled platforms, expand production and water-handling capacity at existing facilities, and develop new natural gas pipeline infrastructure connecting future wells to existing gathering systems. Over the project’s operating life, Arena estimates the improvements could unlock approximately 125 million barrels of additional oil and 250 billion cubic feet of natural gas. “The Southern Eugene Island area is one of the most prolific oil-producing regions in American history, and its infrastructure still has decades of productive life ahead,” said Mike Minarovic, Arena Energy’s founder and CEO. “What it needed was long-term capital to match the opportunity.” The financing represents a notable shift in the federal government’s approach to energy infrastructure lending. Previously known as the Loan Programs Office, the DOE financing program became a major source of federal support for clean energy projects, including renewable power, battery manufacturing and electric vehicles. Under the Trump administration, the renamed office has placed greater emphasis on conventional energy production, grid reliability and reinvestment in existing infrastructure. The Arena loan is the first to reach financial close specifically supporting domestic oil and gas production under the department’s lending programs, according to DOE. “The United States is the world’s largest producer and exporter of oil and natural gas, and thanks to President Trump, American energy production will continue to grow,” Energy Secretary Chris Wright said. “Project Elkhorn will increase oil production by up to 38,600 barrels per day and create thousands of jobs,” Wright added. Arena currently produces approximately 30,000 barrels of oil per day from its offshore Gulf operations, according to DOE. The projected increase from Project Elkhorn would therefore represent a substantial expansion relative to the company’s existing oil production. The project is also expected to support 2,800 jobs, including 2,400 construction positions and 400 operations roles. Arena estimates the additional production will generate approximately $1.6 billion in federal royalty revenue over the life of the project, although that figure represents the company’s projection rather than a guaranteed return on the government’s financing. Founded in 1999, Arena Energy is among the largest privately held offshore oil and natural gas producers in the Gulf. The company says it has invested more than $5 billion in the region and paid more than $1.8 billion in federal royalties since its founding. Arena will execute Project Elkhorn alongside affiliated companies White Fleet Drilling and Rosefield Pipeline. The company said the loan closed following technical, legal, environmental and financial due diligence. Additional financial terms were not disclosed. The investment highlights a growing focus on extending production from mature offshore fields, where existing platforms, pipelines and processing facilities can be refurbished to support additional drilling and production without requiring entirely new offshore developments. articles.body: Russian Diesel Tanker Awaits Destination Off US East Coast Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 10, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Kalyakan A tanker carrying the first cargo of Russian diesel for the United States has come to a halt off the US east coast, shipping data showed on Tuesday, with its operator saying its destination had not yet been decided. President Donald Trump last month announced a surprise deal with Moscow to import diesel from Russia to help lower prices at the pumps ahead of this month's US midterm elections. The Malta-flagged tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel in Russia's Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, LSEG shipping data showed, with an expected delivery date of November 7. But the Greece-based company which manages Agioi Fanendes, Eastmed, said a week later that the vessel was proceeding awaiting orders and that a port of discharge had not yet been nominated or finalised. "Nothing has changed regarding the vessel's destination, she is still awaiting orders," Greece-based vessel manager Eastmed told Reuters on Tuesday. Vessels may change their declared destination or revert to "for orders" status more than once during a voyage when a prospective deal falls through, plans change or the operator does not wish to declare its intended destination. Other tankers carrying Russian diesel which had signalled the US Atlantic Coast as their destination later altered course, shipping data showed. RUSSIAN IMPORTS BANNED IN 2022 Former President Joe Biden had imposed a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Trump in approving the deal last month waived parts of a new US sanctions law on Moscow and said Russia would immediately export 300,000 tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter". New Jersey's Democratic Governor Mikie Sherrill this month warned local port officials and terminal operators against accepting Russian diesel, saying those shipments would break federal law. Sherrill said importing Russian diesel could expose businesses and individuals using New Jersey ports to "harsh" civil and criminal penalties. (Reuters)

"It is important to have it now up and running and therefore we want to have clear timelines for its completion and we want to offer a dedicated funding of 50 million euros to this Black Sea maritime security hub," von der Leyen said at a press conference alongside Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev. articles.title: C.H. Robinson warns of persistent port and drayage constraints
articles.summary: U.S. container ports continue to face inland transportation challenges despite signs of moderating import demand, according to C.H. Robinson’s November 2026 Edge Report. The logistics company highlights pressure on rail connections, chassis availability and terminal access. These constraints continue to affect...
articles.body: U.S. container ports continue to face inland transportation challenges despite signs of moderating import demand, according to C.H. Robinson’s November 2026 Edge Report. The logistics company highlights pressure on rail connections, chassis availability and terminal access. These constraints continue to affect container deliveries, even where vessel operations are running relatively smoothly. In its latest ports and drayage outlook , C.H. Robinson warns that lower import volumes may not immediately improve inland transportation capacity. Instead, uneven vessel arrivals and longer container dwell times can increase demand for trucks, equipment and terminal appointments. Rail delays and chassis shortages pressure US gateways Southern California remains a key area of concern. According to figures cited from the Pacific Merchant Shipping Association, rail-bound import containers at Los Angeles and Long Beach spent an average of 7.19 days at marine terminals in September. By comparison, truck-bound imports recorded an average dwell time of 3.18 days. Limited railcar availability has contributed to these delays, increasing pressure on terminal space and inland delivery schedules. Meanwhile, Savannah continues to experience chassis availability challenges. Containers remaining in circulation for longer periods reduce the number of times each chassis can be used. C.H. Robinson notes that these extended equipment cycles are contributing to higher private chassis costs. Houston faces different pressures. Strong industrial demand, longer inland transportation distances and road congestion continue to affect drayage costs and equipment availability. The report suggests that these conditions could limit the seasonal relief normally expected as import demand slows. Norfolk terminal changes add operational pressure Terminal access restrictions are also affecting container movements at the Port of Virginia. Since October 13, inbound truck gates at Norfolk International Terminals and Virginia International Gateway have operated under shorter access windows. Inbound portals now close at 4 p.m., while mandatory PRO-PASS reservation hours end at 3 p.m. The final refrigerated container pickup is scheduled for 3:30 p.m. According to C.H. Robinson, these changes reduce the flexibility available to trucking companies when collecting containers. Late cargo releases or terminal queues may prevent drivers from completing additional pickups during the same working day. The impact can extend to warehouse appointments, chassis positioning and empty-container returns, potentially adding storage and transportation costs. Beyond North America, the company’s November ocean freight outlook also highlights risks linked to the gradual return of container services through the Suez Canal. Shorter routes may improve vessel circulation, but overlapping arrivals from Suez and Cape of Good Hope services could temporarily increase pressure on European terminals and inland networks. C.H. Robinson expects local infrastructure and equipment constraints to remain important factors in container logistics through the final months of 2026. The report advises shippers to consider terminal access, chassis availability and inland delivery conditions alongside ocean freight schedules when planning shipments.

articles.title: Bureau Veritas upgrades VeriSTAR Green emissions platform

articles.body: Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore has launched an upgraded version of its VeriSTAR Green platform. The new version helps shipping companies manage emissions data, meet environmental regulations and monitor fleet performance. The platform brings reporting and compliance tools into one digital system. Shipowners, operators, managers and charterers can use it to collect information and assess their environmental obligations. In addition, the update introduces improved data sharing and simulation tools. These features help users understand how fuel choices and vessel operations may affect emissions and compliance costs. Improved data sharing and reporting One of the main upgrades is the integration of the Operational Vessel Data (OVD) standard. This framework provides a common format for collecting and sharing operational information. As a result, shipowners, managers, charterers and software providers can exchange data more consistently. The platform also includes automated checks to identify potential errors and improve data quality. VeriSTAR Green supports several environmental regulations, including EU MRV, EU ETS, UK ETS and FuelEU Maritime. It also covers IMO DCS, CII, EEXI, EEDI and SEEMP requirements. Users can work with one dataset to support reporting across these different frameworks. Furthermore, the platform connects with ship monitoring software to transfer operational and emissions data automatically. According to Bureau Veritas, these functions aim to reduce reporting inconsistencies and simplify compliance procedures. New tools help assess carbon costs The upgraded VeriSTAR Green also provides enhanced simulation tools for EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime. These tools allow shipping companies to compare different operational and fuel scenarios. They can then assess the possible effects on compliance requirements and related costs. The platform also includes tools for evaluating CII performance and EEXI requirements. Meanwhile, VeriSTAR Green supports third-party statements covering EU Allowance recovery, FuelEU penalties and compliance balance pooling arrangements. This helps owners, operators and charterers use emissions data when reviewing financial obligations and planning fleet operations. Alex Gregg-Smith, President of Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore, said shipping companies increasingly need reliable emissions information. He explained that the updated platform aims to improve data quality and make compliance management more efficient. Bureau Veritas developed the new version using feedback from customers during its pilot phase. However, the company has not disclosed how many vessels currently use the upgraded system. The update expands the platform’s existing capabilities as shipping companies prepare for changing environmental requirements.

articles.summary: Fifty-one years ago today, the SS Edmund Fitzgerald disappeared beneath the waters of Lake Superior during a powerful November storm, taking all 29 crew members with her in one of...

Join the leading maritime news network The SS Edmund Fitzgerald underway on the Great Lakes. The 729-foot freighter sank in Lake Superior on November 10, 1975, with the loss of all 29 crew members. (Photo: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers) Fifty-one years ago today, the SS Edmund Fitzgerald disappeared beneath the waters of Lake Superior during a powerful November storm, taking all 29 crew members with her in one of the most enduring tragedies in Great Lakes maritime history. The 729-foot freighter sank on November 10, 1975, about 17 miles north-northwest of Whitefish Point, Michigan. No distress call was issued, no survivors were found, and the exact circumstances of her final moments remain a subject of debate more than half a century later. On Tuesday, the Great Lakes Shipwreck Historical Society will mark the 51st anniversary with a private memorial ceremony for surviving family members and others connected to the ship and its crew. The 7 p.m. ceremony at Whitefish Point will be livestreamed. The Edmund Fitzgerald was among the largest and best-known freighters operating on the Great Lakes when she departed Superior, Wisconsin, on November 9, 1975, carrying more than 26,000 long tons of taconite iron ore pellets bound for Detroit. Launched in 1958, the vessel had spent 17 years hauling iron ore across the lakes, serving the steel mills that helped power America’s industrial economy. At 729 feet, she was the largest vessel on the Great Lakes when she entered service. On her final voyage, the Fitzgerald , commanded by Capt. Ernest M. McSorley, was accompanied across Lake Superior by the freighter Arthur M. Anderson . As a powerful autumn storm swept across the lake, conditions deteriorated. According to the National Weather Service , winds reached 50 knots, with waves approaching 20 feet. By the afternoon of November 10, the Fitzgerald had reported damage and was taking on water, though the crew did not indicate that the vessel was in immediate danger. The Anderson , following behind, maintained radio contact as the ships made their way toward the shelter of Whitefish Bay. Shortly after 7:10 p.m., the Fitzgerald disappeared from radar. She had gone down without issuing a distress call. The loss prompted an extensive search, but none of the 29 men aboard survived. The cause of the sinking has never been established beyond dispute. A U.S. Coast Guard investigation concluded that the most probable cause was flooding of the cargo hold through ineffective hatch closures. Other theories have focused on structural failure, grounding and the effects of exceptionally large waves. The tragedy also prompted closer scrutiny of Great Lakes vessel safety, including hatch-cover integrity, loading practices and storm-weather operations. The wreck lies in Canadian waters, where it remains a protected gravesite. In 1995, an expedition recovered the ship’s 200-pound bronze bell, which is now displayed at the Great Lakes Shipwreck Museum at Whitefish Point as a permanent memorial to the crew. The disaster became part of American and Canadian popular culture through Gordon Lightfoot’s 1976 ballad, The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald , which introduced generations of listeners to the story of the ship and the men who died aboard her. Lightfoot died in 2023, but his song remains closely associated with the annual remembrance. This year’s commemorations will also include a ceremony at Split Rock Lighthouse in Minnesota, where the names of all 29 crew members will be read aloud to the tolling of a ship’s bell before the lighthouse beacon is illuminated in their honor. For the maritime community, the anniversary is also a reminder of the hazards faced by crews navigating the Great Lakes, particularly during the powerful storms of late autumn. More than five decades after the sinking, the Edmund Fitzgerald remains the largest vessel ever lost on the Great Lakes. And each November 10, the story returns to the 29 mariners who never made it home. articles.title: AI at Sea: From Connecting Vessels to Measurable Value
articles.summary: When artificial intelligence (AI) and digitalization are discussed in maritime, attention still gravitates toward autonomous ships. Yet the market is not about de-crewing but, rather, applying vessel and shore data to make operations safer, more fuel-efficient…
articles.body: AI at Sea: From Connecting Vessels to Measurable Value Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Alisa Reiner , Contributor Alisa Reiner is an independent contributor. Alisa brings experience in both... November 10, 2026 Copyright MarineLink.com | Photo by Greg Trauthwein modified with ChatGPT When artificial intelligence (AI) and digitalization are discussed in maritime, attention still gravitates toward autonomous ships. Yet the market is not about de-crewing but, rather, applying vessel and shore data to make operations safer, more fuel-efficient, and easier to maintain. As of 2024, the maritime AI market stood at $4.13 billion, with a projected five-year CAGR of 23%. Market-size estimates should be treated cautiously, but the direction is hard to miss – AI solutions have advanced from trials into voyage planning, machinery monitoring, bridge decision support, port coordination, and digital assurance. The main questions are where it is producing measurable operational value and where the evidence still lags the marketing. The Vessel Has to Be Connected First AI does not create useful ship data – it consumes it. The connected vessel is thus a prerequisite for the AI-capable vessel. Propulsion load, fuel flow, vibration, temperature, pressure, weather, satellite, radar, and camera data are collected through the Internet of Things (IoT) sensors and existing shipboard systems, aggregated and pre-processed onboard, and transmitted to shore via secure communications links. Data quality and context set the ceiling on model performance. Sensor drift, missing values, inconsistent naming, and different operating profiles can affect the lab-tested solution reliability. Latency is another factor – any critical computer vision or machinery control cannot rely on continuous cloud connectivity, so the processing must happen on board. AI and digitalization should not be confused with automation in general. Maritime systems are usually a combination of physics-based models, optimization, rules, and machine learning, not a black-box approach. And sensors, inspection, and edge computing are as important as modeling. Leading companies focus on high-value and repeated use cases, hardware-software-AI integration, and actual customer data. AI and digital tools also serve buyers differently. Table 1 maps key needs to the technologies most directly associated with them, distinguishing shipbuilders’ priorities from those of ship operators. Table 1. What shipowners and shipbuilders want from AI, digitalization, and enabling tools Source: author's analysis Where the Numbers Are Already Visible One of the clearest commercial applications is voyage optimization because fuel consumption provides an immediate KPI. In February 2026, NAPA Voyage Optimization trials demonstrated fuel savings of up to 7.1% on both long and shorter voyages. On the separate 34-day Lila Global voyage from Suez to China, NAPA reported $40,200 in voyage cost savings, 35 tons of fuel saved, 106.5 tons of CO2 avoided, and almost one day less steaming time compared to the simulated standard route. These case studies illustrate why voyage optimization is being scaled – even low-single-digit percentages matter at the fleet level. Computer vision on the bridge is also moving beyond pilots. A 2026 Orca AI study covered 139 vessels and more than 10.8 million nautical miles. High-severity close encounters fell 52% between the early adaptation period and months 10-12. Lloyd's Register separately tested Orca AI on an 828-nautical-mile Mediterranean voyage — across 739 targets, the system achieved 94% precision and 98.6% recall, including small and low-radar-signature craft, with no system downtime. It does not mean that AI should substitute the officer on watch, but machine vision can provide an additional layer of attention when humans, radar, and Automatic Identification System (AIS) face certain limitations. Maintenance presents another application with a measurable business case. Wärtsilä reports that AI-enabled diagnostics reduced unscheduled maintenance by 25% on average, 90% of issues were resolved remotely, and 80% within 24 hours. The operating model here matters – AI detects weak signals and anomalies while engineers validate the diagnosis and reaction. The product thus is not a single algorithm but a combination of sensors, analytics, and expertise. Physical AI is also entering inspection and sustainment. Wall-climbing robots of Gecko Robotics are equipped with ultrasonic sensors to inspect the steel structure of vessels and collect data on its thickness and defects related to corrosion and degradation. In a U.S. Navy application, the system collected more than 4.2 million data points versus around 100 using traditional inspection methods, while a ship-rudder inspection fell from 11 days to one. The data feed digital condition models for maintenance planning and drydock decisions. This example shows another domain where physical AI produces value – by combining robotics with AI-driven analysis of data. Beyond the Ship Ports are another natural target due to the abundance of data on arrival times, berth availability, traffic, weather, and terminal capacity. A 2026 peer-reviewed study of an AI-enabled Just-In-Time (JIT) arrival system reported simulated fuel and emissions savings of 6.45%-7.39% where earlier coordination allowed ships to slow down. Digital twins and data-driven health management are in a similar space – they compare actual behavior of machinery to the expected one to detect deterioration prior to failure. In May 2026, Lloyd's Register granted Approval in Principle to Navantia's AI-based Digital Twin Ready framework. In September 2026, LR also awarded AiP to HD KSOE's VesselWise autonomous auxiliary-machinery optimization function, with onboard validation planned on a 174,000-cbm LNG carrier. AI in maritime is moving from monitoring towards machinery optimization, but the assurance follows closely. Generative AI is less mature operationally. It can make manuals, maintenance histories, and fleet data more searchable or assist shore teams with anomalies investigation. But for now, hard maritime KPI evidence is still scarce in this field, and errors in safety-critical workflows can be costly. Taken together, these examples illustrate the variety of maritime AI applications and their different levels of maturity and autonomy. Figure 1. Maritime AI and digital tools applications: commercial maturity vs degree of autonomous action. Source: author's analytical assessment based on public deployment. Scores are comparative, The Hype Gap Is Mostly a Systems Problem One of the major obstacles to using AI in maritime is not access to a model but integration. AI works in a closed loop – sensors generate data, the model discovers/predicts something valuable, someone makes the decision or controls systems according to the results, and outcomes become feedback. Any disconnected data or process break this loop. The importance of cybersecurity grows as the loop closes. The connected maintenance platform is different from a spreadsheet, and AI integrated with navigation or machinery affects physical operations. IMO has repeatedly highlighted cyber risk across shipboard IT and operational technology. Sensor spoofing, corrupted data, compromised communications, and unauthorized access are therefore not separate IT issues – they are operational risks. Human factors matter too. Too many alerts create alarm fatigue, unexplained recommendations may be ignored, and models can fail in unusual conditions. Crew training, interface design, decision responsibility, and fallback procedures are no less important than model accuracy. From Fancy Tools to Operating System Commercial applications include voyage and speed optimization, computer-vision watchkeeping, condition-based maintenance, and fleet analytics. They solve repetitive, data-rich problems measurable with KPIs on fuel, safety, or downtime. The second group requires proving at scale – autonomous machinery control, AI-enabled digital twins, robotic inspection, generative copilots and highly autonomous ships. With AI moving closer to physical control, validation, cybersecurity, and class approval become more important. For shipowners, the relevant question is not “Do we have AI?” but the decision affected, the data backing it, result measurement, and actions in case of error or offline mode. The winning applications would be those that make a few expensive decisions better. Ultimately, digital tools and AI can help with detection and analysis, but human expertise would still be needed to interpret outputs, take decisions, and apply insights in practice. ▪ Sources 1. Given the scale and complexity of these operations, every decision affects thousands of containers...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Gregor Fischer Hapag-Lloyd, the world’s fifth-largest container carrier, operates 300 vessels on 133 liner services, transporting 13.5 million twenty-foot-equivalent units a year between 600 ports worldwide. Given the scale and complexity of these operations, every decision affects thousands of containers per vessel – with the consequences of any misstep felt throughout the supply chain. The company’s proactive approach to fleetwide digitalisation has therefore been devised with one overarching objective in mind: to simplify its operations. According to Patrick Briest, Hapag-Lloyd’s Senior Director of Operations and IT Products,digitalisation “can do many things”, but making things simpler – from both a commercial and operational perspective – is its one “superpower”. Digitalisation and the connectivity that supports it are increasingly judged by concrete commercial and operational outcomes. “We don’t digitalise just because we can,” Briest told the audience at a recent Inmarsat ‘Connected to Perform’ seminar during SMM 2026. “We digitalise because there’s a use case for it – because there’s value we can drive.” For Hapag-Lloyd, tangible targets include maintaining schedule reliability above 90% across its network, reducing emissions per TEU by 30% by 2030, and approaching net-zero emissions by 2045 – all while cutting operating costs by approximately $100 per TEU. Achieving these goals will require tapping into the “superpower” of digitalisation to facilitate faster and better-informed decisions, said Briest: “We want to enable ourselves, our people, to decide faster, decide better – because we’ve got the data and the tools to understand the impact of every one of the little operational decisions we make all the time.” To illustrate the benefits of digitalisation and connectivity on Hapag-Lloyd’s operations, Briest presented a notional voyage involving a container ship transporting perishable goods from the west coast of South America to Northern Europe. If a crane were to fail during the vessel’s final port call in South America, he said, the consequentdelays might result in the ship missing its slot to cross the Panama Canal. However, by retrieving operational data from the vessel’s digital cargo logbook, Hapag-Lloyd would know by exactly how long to extend its port call to maximise cargo intake without sacrificing its slot. Later, if the vessel were to encounter extreme weather in the Atlantic Ocean, the operator would combine specific vessel data points with shore-based analysis to evaluate routing, speed, fuel consumption, and port arrival options. In this way, Briest explained, Hapag-Lloyd could keep commercial and environmental impacts to a minimum without compromising voyage safety. Digitalisation and connectivity, then, enable shipping companies like Hapag-Lloyd to make smarter operational decisions based on a richer and more immediate view of what is happening on the vessel and across the network. As Briest demonstrated in the second scenario, they also help close the gap between ship and shore. In another example, IT support teams can now connect directly with the vessel, remotely accessing even the engine room to help resolve technical issues efficiently. Whereas ships previously operated as isolated assets, they increasingly function as an extension of head office, with seafarers and shorestaff working as one team, and the Atlantic Ocean – in Briest’s words – becoming “as connected as downtown Frankfurt”. Digitalisation is connecting vessels not only to their operator’s headquarters but also with the clientswhose goods they transport. In a further operational scenario from the notional voyage, Briest explained that the Hapag-Lloyd LIVE tool allows customers to monitor refrigerated cargo and respond when circumstances change. If the vessel is delayed, temperature settings can be adjusted remotely to help ensure the cargo reaches its destination in optimal condition. “By being more digital, we want to be as easy to do business with for our customers as we possibly can be,” he commented. Recognising that increased connectivity also has its challenges, Hapag-Lloyd’s digitalisation strategy emphasises cybersecurity and seafarer autonomy to maintain operational resilience. “As we connect more systems on the vessel, we’re of course creating a substantially bigger attack surface,” Briest acknowledged, adding that the company is “pushing between 100 and 200 patches to every vessel every week” to address this issue. Cybersecurity, he said, “cannot be an afterthought anymore” – instead, it should be “secure by design and [built] from the ground up”. At the same time, Hapag-Lloyd is taking care to ensure digitalisation strengthens rather than weakens the judgement, resilience, and practical competency of its seafarers. “Digitalisation can help a lot, but there’s an inherent [seafaring] culture, capability and skillset that we also need to preserve,” said Briest. These considerations become increasingly important as Hapag-Lloyd’s digitalisation strategy progresses. As more decisions, systems, applications, and interactions come to depend on the ship–shore connection, and the vessel is further integrated into the broader digital operating environment, connectivity itself becomes strategic infrastructure. Inmarsat Maritime’s NexusWave is a key enabler of Hapag-Lloyd’s digitalisation strategy. The fully managed, bonded multi-network connectivity solution delivers the consistent high speeds, global reliability, and secure-by-design infrastructure the company needs to continue its transformation and pursue its operational ambitions with confidence. Digitalisation, Briest summarised, is helping Hapag-Lloyd to manage its workload, make better decisions, and work more effectively as a team – both onboard the vessel and between ship and shore. While he stressed that connectivity needs to be managed responsibly to preserve cybersecurity and crew autonomy, he was in no doubt about the direction of travel: “The future of shipping is connected,” he concluded. articles.body: Europe Tankers Rubico targets five-ship MR fleet with latest Top Ships newbuild swoop Adis Ajdin November 11, 2026 0 436 1 minute read GSI GSI Nasdaq-listed Rubico has struck a deal to take another two MR tanker newbuildings from Top Ships in a $14.5m deal, continuing the reshuffle of Evangelos Pistiolis-linked tanker orders in China. The Athens-based owner is buying two special-purpose companies holding shipbuilding contracts for 47,499 dwt product and chemical tankers at Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI). The vessels are scheduled for delivery in the fourth quarters of 2028 and 2029. Both ships have already secured seven-year time charters with Trafigura Maritime Logistics from delivery, with options for a further four years. Including those extensions, the contracts carry potential gross revenue of about $150.9m. The acquisition would take Rubico’s MR newbuilding pipeline to five vessels, with potential charter revenue of approximately $377.1m. Including its operating fleet, the company puts its total potential gross revenue backlog at $523.1m, up around 40%. Rubico will pay $14.5m for the shares in the two companies, either in cash or through its Series G convertible preferred shares, or a combination of both. Completion is expected by March 31, 2027. The vessels also come with sale-and-leaseback financing arranged with a major Chinese leasing house, covering 85% of the shipbuilding instalments at term SOFR plus 1.8%. The latest move adds to a series of deals between Rubico and Pistiolis-led Top Ships this year. Rubico previously acquired three GSI MR newbuilding contracts from its former parent, with the vessels due to join the fleet in 2029. Rubico was spun off from Top Ships in August 2025 with two 157,000 dwt suezmax tankers, Eco Malibu and Eco West Coast . The wider tanker investment drive began in February, when Pistiolis’ privately held Central Group ordered 10 MR tankers at GSI in a deal approaching $500m. Much of that programme has since been moved into the listed shipping companies. articles.title: DHL Express signs SAF supply agreement with TotalEnergies at Paris CDG
articles.summary: DHL Express has signed a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) supply agreement with TotalEnergies for its air cargo operations at Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport. The renewable one-year agreement covers 5 million litres of SAF. It also marks the first use of the alternative fuel by DHL Express in France. The company...
articles.body: DHL Express has signed a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) supply agreement with TotalEnergies for its air cargo operations at Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport. The renewable one-year agreement covers 5 million litres of SAF. It also marks the first use of the alternative fuel by DHL Express in France. The company announced that its first aircraft using SAF departed from Paris Charles de Gaulle on 9 November 2026. The agreement supports DHL’s efforts to reduce emissions from its international express network. SAF to support European air cargo operations Under the agreement, TotalEnergies will supply SAF for aircraft departing from DHL Express’s Paris Charles de Gaulle hub. The flights will connect Paris with DHL’s air hubs in Leipzig, Casablanca, Milan and London. According to DHL, the initiative is expected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 11,800 metric tons of CO₂ equivalent annually. SAF can be produced from waste and residual materials, including used cooking oil. It can also be blended with conventional aviation fuel and used in existing aircraft without major infrastructure changes. Depending on the feedstock and production process, SAF can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by around 80% compared with conventional jet fuel. However, this figure refers to emissions across the fuel’s lifecycle rather than an equivalent reduction in emissions from each individual flight. Travis Cobb, EVP Global Network Operations & Aviation at DHL Express, said the agreement forms part of the company’s wider strategy to reduce emissions from international express transportation. He also noted that SAF represented 10% of the aviation fuel used across DHL’s own aircraft fleet in 2025. SAF volumes to support GoGreen Plus DHL will incorporate the SAF volumes into its GoGreen Plus service, which helps customers address transport-related greenhouse gas emissions. The programme uses a book-and-claim system to allocate verified emissions reductions to participating customers. As a result, customers can receive the environmental benefits of sustainable fuels even when their shipments are not transported on the aircraft using those fuels. The initiative is also expected to support customers managing Scope 3 emissions associated with transportation and distribution. Meanwhile, the agreement coincides with the fifth anniversary of DHL Express’s Paris Charles de Gaulle hub. Opened in 2021 following an investment of €170 million, the facility is a major part of the company’s European air cargo network. The hub operates around the clock and can process up to 38,000 parcels and documents per hour. Through the new agreement, DHL Express and TotalEnergies are expanding the use of sustainable aviation fuel in European express logistics, while linking the associated emissions benefits to DHL’s customer decarbonisation services.

articles.body: Asia Dry Cargo Europe Finance and Insurance Greater China Shipping heavyweights back Cetus $175m Oslo listing Adis Ajdin November 11, 2026 0 368 1 minute read Cetus Maritime Cetus Maritime Hong Kong-based dry bulk owner Cetus Maritime has lined up some of shipping’s biggest investment names for a $175m private placement ahead of its planned Oslo listing later this month. An investment vehicle linked to Idan Ofer’s Eastern Pacific Shipping, Arne Blystad’s Songa Capital and the Albemarle Shipping Fund, co-founded by Magnus Halvorsen, are among investors that have indicated interest in the share issue. Together with DNB Asset Management, the four parties have signalled interest in subscribing for a combined $106.5m. Cetus said additional indications from other investors were sufficient to cover the entire offering before launch. The Mark Young-led company is looking to issue about 95.6m new shares at $1.83 apiece, with an option to increase the placement by another $25m. The pricing values Cetus at around $239m before the fundraising and its planned fleet acquisition. That rises to approximately $307m once the transaction is taken into account. The company is targeting its first day of trading on Euronext Growth Oslo around November 18. Clarksons Securities, DNB Carnegie and Nordea are handling the placement and listing process. The move follows Cetus’s agreement to expand its fleet through a transaction with Hong Kong-listed Seacon Shipping Group, covering 13 handysize and ultramax bulkers, alongside the acquisition of Syngrace, which holds shipbuilding contracts for three additional handysize vessels. The latest transaction terms call for approximately $72.5m in cash and the issue of 37.3m Cetus shares. Following the acquisition and a planned vessel sale, Cetus expects to have 42 ships in its fleet, comprising 34 vessels on the water and eight newbuildings scheduled for delivery in 2027 and 2028. Cetus was formed through the merger of Asia Maritime Pacific and Hamburg Bulk Carriers in 2023, before combining with Chile’s Nachipa the following year. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo A vessel operated by ADNOC Logistics & Services was damaged in an attack in UAE territorial waters on Tuesday, as maritime authorities reported a separate apparent projectile strike against a tanker near the Strait of Hormuz, adding to a growing series of attacks on commercial shipping in the region. ADNOC Logistics & Services confirmed that one of its vessels sustained damage in an attack in the Persian Gulf on the afternoon of November 10. In a statement carried by the UAE’s state-run WAM news agency, the company said response operations were ongoing but provided no details about the vessel’s identity, the extent of the damage or whether any crew members were injured. The company said further updates would be provided as information became available. The announcement came as the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that a tanker had been struck by an unidentified projectile approximately 19 nautical miles northeast of Lima, Oman, near the strategically important Strait of Hormuz. According to UKMTO Warning 201-26 , the incident occurred at 1338 UTC on November 10. The vessel’s master reported that all crew members were safe and there was no environmental impact. A damage assessment was planned for first light. UKMTO did not identify the tanker or establish the origin of the projectile. It was not immediately clear whether the ADNOC incident and the strike reported by UKMTO were connected or represented separate attacks. The latest developments follow a series of incidents along the Omani side of the Strait of Hormuz, where vessels have faced projectile strikes, fires and other hostile activity in recent days. On November 7, a tanker caught fire approximately eight nautical miles northwest of Khasab, Oman, forcing its crew to evacuate. UKMTO initially reported the incident based on information from military authorities before subsequently reclassifying it as an attack . Another tanker transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz was reportedly struck by an unidentified projectile on November 7. Its crew was reported safe, with no environmental impact. The incidents come as maritime security authorities continue to warn of an exceptionally dangerous operating environment in and around the strait. In its November 8 advisory , the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) maintained the threat level for the Strait of Hormuz at SEVERE, warning that further deliberate attacks were highly likely. JMIC reported five attacks off Oman’s Musandam coast between November 1 and November 5, followed by additional incidents on November 7. The center said 177 maritime security incidents had been recorded across the wider region since March 1. That figure includes suspicious activity and military enforcement incidents, rather than attacks against merchant vessels alone. Commercial traffic through the waterway remains far below normal levels. According to JMIC, independent tracking indicated daily transits in the single digits to low double digits, compared with a historical average of approximately 138 vessels per day in 2025. U.S. naval shipping coordination figures, meanwhile, indicated 91 U.S.-facilitated transits between November 5 and 7, averaging roughly 30 per day. The figures reflect different reporting systems and vessel populations and are not directly comparable. The disruption has left large numbers of vessels waiting outside the waterway. JMIC estimated that approximately 162 ships were anchored near Fujairah and Khor Fakkan as of November 8, with additional concentrations near Sohar and Musandam. The center warned that continued attacks, Iranian monitoring of commercial shipping and U.S. naval blockade enforcement were likely to keep shipping operators cautious and traffic depressed. Tuesday’s reported attacks add to mounting concerns over the safety of merchant vessels and their crews in one of the world’s most important energy shipping corridors, where repeated security incidents continue to complicate commercial transit despite efforts to facilitate vessel movements. articles.body: Marlink Secures BV Certification for XChange NextGen Platform Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 10, 2026 © Marlink Marlink has secured Bureau Veritas (BV) type approval for the XChange NextGen edge platform, giving shipowners independent assurance that their onboard digital infrastructure is designed with long-term cyber resilience built-in. For shipowners, onboard technology is a long-term investment that can remain in service for years. As software evolves and new services are introduced, cybersecurity must remain a priority throughout the platform’s lifecycle. XChange NextGen’s type approval confirms compliance with requirements covering both cybersecurity capabilities and the processes supporting secure development, maintenance and updates. XChange NextGen is Marlink’s onboard platform, combining edge computing with connectivity, network orchestration, cybersecurity and cloud services to support secure digital operations. Its edge capability allows data to be processed on board, giving shipowners a foundation for analytics and AI applications that depend on reliable data flow between vessel and shore. As part of the Marlink Possibility Portfolio, it reduces hardware complexity and enables vessel and shore teams to deploy, manage and scale digital services more easily across fleets. The certification confirms compliance with IACS UR E27 Rev.1 and Bureau Veritas NR659 requirements within the approved scope. While IACS UR E26 addresses cyber resilience at vessel level, UR E27 focuses on individual onboard systems and equipment, providing shipowners, shipyards and systems integrators with evidence to support applicable class requirements. XChange NextGen’s E27 type approval complements Marlink’s wider approach to vessel cyber resilience. Its OT Security offering helps shipowners identify and manage cyber risks in operational systems, supporting their broader work to meet applicable vessel-level requirements, including IACS UR E26.

articles.body: Boluda Shipping has signed an agreement to acquire Matrans Terminal in Rotterdam, strengthening its planned expansion into Northern Europe. The agreement was signed on 3 November 2026 and covers the multipurpose terminal in Eemhaven, an important hub for European short-sea shipping. The transaction follows Boluda Shipping’s recent agreement to acquire Samskip . Both acquisitions remain subject to regulatory approvals and other closing conditions. The Matrans deal will give Boluda additional port infrastructure in Rotterdam as it seeks to expand its maritime and intermodal logistics activities. Matrans adds terminal and rail capabilities Matrans Terminal covers approximately 360,000 square metres, including 70,000 square metres of covered warehousing. The facility offers 1,100 metres of quay with a water depth of 12.65 metres. It also includes a Ro-Ro berth with a depth of nine metres and 600 metres of railway track. The terminal handles containers, general cargo, forest products, metals, project cargo and Ro-Ro shipments. In addition, Matrans provides customs services, fiscal representation, road transport and freight forwarding. These activities support cargo movements between the port and inland destinations. Boluda Shipping plans to develop the terminal’s operations, with a focus on improving efficiency, increasing cargo volumes and expanding customer services. However, the company has not disclosed the financial terms of the acquisition. Rotterdam supports Northern European expansion The Matrans agreement forms part of Boluda Shipping’s wider strategy to strengthen its presence in Northern Europe. The company already operates in the region through Boluda Towage and its maritime transport and logistics activities. It also opened new offices in Rotterdam in June 2026. Following completion of the planned acquisitions, Boluda Shipping expects its international network to comprise 21 maritime terminals and five rail terminals. The expanded infrastructure would support connections between short-sea shipping, rail transport and road distribution. Rotterdam is expected to play an important role in coordinating these services and connecting Northern European markets with the Iberian Peninsula, the Canary Islands and West Africa. For Boluda, adding Matrans would provide additional cargo-handling and storage capacity at a major European gateway. The terminal’s rail facilities could also support the development of multimodal transport services. Both the Matrans and Samskip acquisitions remain subject to the necessary approvals. Until the transactions are completed, the announced network expansion remains conditional.

articles.title: Cflow Provides Fish Handling System for Brønnbåt Wellboat
articles.summary: Brønnbåt Nord's largest wellboat to date will be equipped with a complete fish handling system from Cflow in Langevåg, on Norway's west coast. The solutions have been further developed to ensure good conditions for the fish, gentler handling…
articles.body: Cflow Provides Fish Handling System for Brønnbåt Wellboat Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 10, 2026 © Cflow Brønnbåt Nord's largest wellboat to date will be equipped with a complete fish handling system from Cflow in Langevåg, on Norway's west coast. The solutions have been further developed to ensure good conditions for the fish, gentler handling and efficient operations on board. With a cargo capacity of 5,000 cubic meters, the new wellboat can carry the equivalent of approximately 4.2 million salmon dinners in a single trip to the processing plant. The investment will help meet growing demand for wellboat capacity in Northern Norway. Brønnbåt Nord is owned by the aquaculture companies Salaks, Gratanglaks and Kleiva Fiskefarm. The vessel has been designed by NSK Ship Design in Harstad and will be built at Zamakona Shipyard in Bilbao, Spain, with delivery scheduled for 2029. The newbuild will feature battery-hybrid propulsion, an energy-efficient hull design and the capacity to produce up to 10,000 cubic meters of freshwater on board. The new vessel will be equipped with several further-developed Cflow solutions designed to ensure good water quality and greater control over the conditions fish are exposed to during transport and handling. Cflow's delivery includes complete systems for fish handling, water circulation and treatment, hygiene, automation and data logging. It also features high-capacity CO2 degassing systems, systems for regulating total gas pressure (TGP), and nanobubble generators from Cflow's partner Moleaer, which supply oxygen to the water. The nanobubble generators inject very small oxygen bubbles that remain in the water for longer, rather than quickly rising to the surface. According to Cflow, this enables more efficient use of oxygen compared with traditional venturi injectors. The vessel will be equipped with fish loading and unloading lines with a diameter of 600 millimeters (DN600), designed to handle high capacities during loading and unloading. This will enable efficient fish handling and shorter operation times, while keeping fish welfare a key priority. Cflow will also deliver piping systems designed for cleaning in place (CIP), without the need for dismantling. This will simplify cleaning procedures and help maintain good hygiene between operations. In addition, the vessel will be equipped with fish counters from Wingtech, adapted for different operations on board. The counters will record the number of fish during loading and unloading, and one of the counters will also be suitable for smolt counting. This will give the shipping company better control over the number of fish being handled. Cflow and Brønnbåt Nord previously collaborated on the battery-hybrid wellboat MS Caspian , delivered in 2024. Experience gained from that project has been carried forward into the development of solutions for the new vessel. Although the vessel will be built in Spain, approximately 40 per cent of the deliveries will come from Norwegian companies. For Cflow, based in Langevåg near Alesund, the contract means significant activity in the years ahead, helping to support local employment and further development of the company's technology expertise.

articles.body: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Tuesday, 10 November, that two oil tankers had caught fire following explosions while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz through routes not authorised by Tehran. According to a statement carried by Iranian news agency Tasnim , one of the vessels, described as a supertanker, allegedly struck a naval mine, triggering an explosion and subsequent fire. The second tanker reportedly experienced a separate incident while attempting to cross the waterway under the alleged protection of US military aircraft. The IRGC claimed that both vessels had switched off their navigation and identification systems before attempting the passage. The tankers were subsequently left immobilised and burning near the southern coast of the strait, according to the statement. Iranian authorities did not disclose the names, flags or ownership of either vessel, while no details were provided regarding their crews, potential casualties or the extent of the reported damage. The circumstances surrounding the incidents, including the alleged US military involvement, have not been independently verified. Maritime security concerns continue The latest announcement follows a series of similar claims by Iranian authorities concerning tankers attempting to use routes that Tehran considers unauthorised. On 5 November, the IRGC reported that two oil tankers and a tugboat had caught fire in separate incidents in the Strait of Hormuz. Further claims involving vessels striking naval mines were made in the following days. With vessel identities remaining undisclosed, it is unclear whether the latest announcement refers to entirely separate incidents. The situation comes amid continued restrictions on commercial navigation through the waterway, which connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and remains a critical corridor for international energy shipments. Earlier this year, Iran established the Persian Gulf Strait Authority , introducing a framework requiring vessels to obtain authorisation before transiting the strategic passage. Commercial shipping has faced mounting security challenges in the region since the escalation of the conflict in late February. In October, the Singapore-registered container ship GFS Pride sank following a projectile strike near the Strait of Hormuz , while another Singapore-registered container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained damage in a separate incident. The latest Iranian claims add to uncertainty surrounding maritime operations in the area, although independent confirmation of the reported tanker incidents remains outstanding.
