articles.title: From basic wave data to trusted predictive decision support
articles.summary: What turns a wave measurement into a prediction your crew can trust?
articles.body: Branded Content November 10, 2026 · 41 minutes ago From basic wave data to trusted predictive decision support What turns a wave measurement into a prediction your crew can trust? Written in partnership with Miros 7 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Start with the operational question: Do you understand the wave conditions around your vessel during operations? Can the crew find the measurement when they need it? Can they explain what significant wave height and wave period mean for this vessel and this task? Source: Miros real-time WaveSystem dashboard showcase (AI Illustration) Author: Lars Ivar Leivestad, Commercial Manager at Miros Picture a vessel holding position offshore. The next operation has been carefully planned, the crew is briefed, and the weather forecast suggests conditions are within operational limits. But then the vessel starts moving more than expected. The sea looks much the same as it did earlier. Is this a temporary variation or a sign of changing sea conditions? Will it now impact the lifting operation, personnel transfer or equipment deployment about to begin? How can the crew make an informed decision about whether to proceed? Local, real-time sea state measurements can help. By providing an accurate picture of the sea conditions around the vessel, they help bridge the gap between forecasts and what is happening offshore. But having access to data is only the first step. The real value comes from understanding the measurements, connecting them to operational decisions and building more advanced capabilities as needs evolve. Start with the operational question: Do you understand the wave conditions around your vessel during operations? Begin with a task the crew recognizes. For a Chief Officer preparing a deck cargo transfer on a platform supply vessel, that might mean understanding the wave conditions along the vessel during the operation. Identify the question and the people who need the answer. One of our offshore vessel customers began with just such a need. They already had forecasts and experienced personnel, but wanted a continuous, measured real-time reference for the local sea state. The first installation used a single non-contact wave sensor, with significant wave height and wave period as the initial parameters. Forecasts remain part of planning. Real-time measurements add information about conditions at the measurement location. Before you add more data, decide what the first measurement is for. Name the decision it should inform. For the Chief Officer, that could be the call on whether to start the deck cargo transfer. Then set a first goal the team can check. Can the crew find the measurement when they need it? Can they explain what significant wave height and wave period mean for this vessel and this task? Are they using it in the go/no-go discussions you identified? Once the answer to each is yes, crew and management share a clear baseline. Know what the number represents: Is the sensor wrong, or are you comparing two different things? Say a larger wave passes the vessel while the significant wave height changes little. Significant wave height, commonly written Hs, is a statistical measure approximately corresponding to the average height of the highest third of waves. Individual waves can be higher. Wave period is the time between successive wave crests passing a fixed point. Displays can present it in more than one way, so confirm which period parameter yours shows. The measurement context is equally important. Identify the sensor location, the area or point it observes, the reporting interval and the quality information available. Understand how the system accounts for vessel motion. A downward-looking range measurement from a moving platform needs appropriate motion compensation to distinguish surface movement from sensor movement. A reading from one point on the vessel does not describe every point around the hull. Check the timestamp and the averaging period used for statistical parameters. Those details help distinguish a live display update from the passage of an individual wave. Ask the watch team to explain the parameter in relation to the task. Significant wave height, commonly written Hs, is a statistical measure approximately corresponding to the average height of the highest third of waves. Individual waves can be higher. The measurement context is important. Source: Miros varying sea condition illustration (AI Illustration) Build confidence through operational use: When the sea changes, what changes on the display? Give the team opportunities to compare measurements with conditions and vessel behavior during normal work. When a measurement seems surprising, review the observation, the parameter definition and the data quality together. In our customer’s initial experience, personnel compared wave readings with what they could see and feel. Over time, they began relating combinations of wave height and period to their vessel’s behavior. A Master and Chief Officer can bring that same learning into a briefing: the measured conditions, the planned task and the relevant operating limits. Recording the conditions and the vessel’s operating state gives later reviews something specific to examine. Visual agreement helps build familiarity, but technical verification is still necessary to confirm measurement performance. Confidence requires both reliable measurements and an understanding of their operational significance. Progress shows when people can explain what the readings mean for their work, identify gaps and raise questions that experience alone or the initial parameters do not fully answer. Add context when the question changes: Why can a familiar significant wave height accompany a different vessel response? Wave period and direction relative to heading can help explain the difference. Waves approaching the bow, beam or stern do not produce the same response in every case. Add directional information when it addresses a specific operational need. Surface current measurement can provide further context for a Dynamic Positioning Officer considering environmental conditions on a construction support vessel. It does not provide a current profile through the water column. This expansion requires the right measurement configuration. Combining X-band radar with a downward-looking wave sensor adds directional wave and surface-current information to the local wave measurements. Before interpreting directional data, confirm the reference frame and conventions in the system documentation. Wave direction must be understood in relation to the vessel’s heading and the operation. The key question: Can users understand and explain the purpose of each additional measurement? Confirm the required equipment, interfaces and data quality before introducing new parameters. Video clip: 3D vessel view 3D interface in Miros WaveSystem, showing where each wave measurement is taken. It brings each installed measurement source, its measurement area and the key wave values together in one intuitive display, providing a bird’s-eye view of the sea state data most relevant to safeguard operations. Source: Miros WaveSystem 3D vessel visualization Connect the waves with the vessel: Which approaching waves and associated motions would be useful to anticipate? Now bring measured vessel response into the discussion. Vessel design, size, loading condition, heading and operating mode all influence how a vessel responds to the sea. Wave height alone cannot describe the implications for every operation. For a service operation vessel preparing a gangway connection, relate the environmental conditions to vessel motions and the applicable equipment and operational limits. For a research or survey vessel recovering an instrument, connect the wave conditions with the motions affecting equipment handling. Assess these relationships in the context of the specific vessel and operation. Keep wave measurements, vessel motions and equipment performance distinct. Understanding one does not automatically establish the others. Identify the motion, such as heave, roll or pitch, and where on the vessel it matters. Measure or predict where it matters. Bring measured vessel response into the discussion. Vessel design, size, loading condition, heading and operating mode all influence how a vessel responds to the sea. Wave height alone cannot describe the implications for every operation. Source: Cable lay vessel, Adobe Stock Evaluate the prediction against actual outcomes: How do you know the prediction is right? Approach prediction with the same discipline as the initial measurements. Establish what is being predicted, how far ahead, under which conditions and with what level of uncertainty. Miros’ PredictifAI technology, for example, combines X-band radar observations of incoming waves, local downward-looking wave measurements and artificial intelligence. It provides deterministic predictions of waves and vessel motion, including when they will occur. The published prediction horizon ranges from seconds to a couple of minutes, depending on installation and operating conditions. Available predicted output depends on the installation. Motions influenced by dynamic positioning, navigation or crane operations cannot automatically be predicted from wave measurements alone. Compare predictions with subsequent measurements to assess their accuracy. Consider the timing and size of the event, the uncertainty involved and the conditions in which the comparison was made. Review the results with relevant personnel before deciding how predictions should support operations. The available prediction might support a critical phase of a lifting operation or a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) deployment. But the prediction horizon alone cannot establish suitability for an entire operation extending beyond it. Understanding the measurements helps users look beyond the “black box.” Confidence starts with reliable input data, but predictions must also demonstrate their accuracy and operational value. Video clip: PredictifAi traffic light display Miros’ PredictifAI technology combines X-band radar observations of incoming waves, local downward-looking wave measurements and artificial intelligence. It provides deterministic wave and vessel motion prediction, from seconds to a couple of minutes, depending on installation and operating conditions. Source: Miros PredictifAI traffic light display Make the information part of the watch The next watch should also be able to use and question the information. Integrate it into training, handovers, toolbox talks and operational reviews, ensuring its role within existing procedures is clear. Establish how personnel should respond when data is unavailable or unreliable. A Marine Operations Manager with access to the same measurements can discuss plans with the offshore team using a shared understanding of conditions. A Marine Superintendent can help integrate the technology into training and procedures, in line with the operator’s defined responsibilities. A Coast Guard vessel preparing to launch or recover a small boat must also consider local sea conditions and vessel motions in the context of the task. Prediction remains one input alongside forecasts, procedures, measured conditions and established operational limits. Qualified personnel retain responsibility for operational decisions. Back on board, the next operation still requires a decision. Better-informed discussions can start with a single trusted measurement, then build toward directional waves, surface currents, vessel response and prediction. Measure. Understand. Trust. Expand. Predict. One trusted measurement. One practical step at a time. Some organizations may benefit from a more comprehensive system from the outset. For those new to wave monitoring, the priority is to establish the value of the initial measurements before expanding. articles.title: First oil from Southeast Asian offshore project flows sooner than expected
articles.summary: The start of production from an offshore platform at an oil field in Vietnamese waters comes 36 days ahead of schedule.
articles.body: Exploration & Production November 10, 2026 · 13 minutes ago First oil from Southeast Asian offshore project flows sooner than expected The start of production from an offshore platform at an oil field in Vietnamese waters comes 36 days ahead of schedule. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Oil production has kicked off from BK-26 platform at Bach Ho field Source: Vietsovpetro Beating its planned start date by more than a month, the Vietnam-Russia joint venture Vietsovpetro has achieved its first oil flow from a wellhead platform at the Bach Ho field off the coast of Vietnam to boost its 2026 output amid natural field declines and strengthen the Southeast Asian country's energy security. The first oil milestone that was recorded on November 9, 2026, has enabled Vietsovpetro to bring online the BK-26 platform at the Bach Ho field in Block 09-1 offshore Vietnam. The beginning of production was achieved 36 days ahead of the approved timeline set by the Intergovernmental Council, because it was originally scheduled for December 15, 2026. The early start-up is interpreted to directly augment domestic crude oil output, strongly supporting the fulfillment of Vietsovpetro and Petrovietnam’s 2026 production and business targets. The project enables field optimization by securing stable, sustainable reservoir extraction and extending the economic life of the offshore Bach Ho field in the coming years. Petrovietnam emphasized: “This achievement highlights Vietsovpetro’s proven project execution capabilities, engineering excellence, and the enduring effectiveness of Vietnam - Russia energy cooperation. "By continuously optimizing offshore infrastructure, Petrovietnam firmly reinforces its mission of safeguarding national energy security.” On November 3, the Vietsovpetro Acceptance Council conducted the overall acceptance of the BK-26 project, issued a decision to put it into use on November 5, and assessed the completion level of the project to ensure operational safety. Since the output at Vietsovpetro's traditional oil fields is in a process of natural decline, Petrovietnam highlights that putting BK-26 into operation ahead of schedule is of great significance. Petrovietnam noted: “The oil flow from BK26 not only marks the introduction of a new project into operation but is also the result of the synchronous coordination process between units participating in the project. “Ensuring progress in offshore construction conditions facing many weather disadvantages, continuing to affirm the ability to master from exploration, design, construction to management, operation and exploitation of offshore oil and gas projects; and at the same time showing the spirit of responsibility and high determination of Vietsovpetro's collective of workers.” Related Articles Fossil Energy Petrovietnam and Gazprom outline drilling plans to boost gas production off Vietnam 2 min read The BK-26 project entails the BK-26 wellhead platform and bridge connecting to MSP-8; MSP-8 renovation to receive and process products from BK-26; and relocation of MSP8-MSP4 underground power cable line. articles.title: Ofgem names preferred bidder for Dogger Bank B offshore transmission assets
articles.summary: A consortium of Diamond Transmission UK (DTUK) and Japan’s Chubu Electric Power has been selected as the preferred bidder to acquire and operate...
articles.body: News November 10, 2026 · 1 minute ago Ofgem names preferred bidder for Dogger Bank B offshore transmission assets AB Adrijana Buljan Offshore Wind 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Dogger Bank Wind Farm A consortium of Diamond Transmission UK (DTUK) and Japan’s Chubu Electric Power has been selected as the preferred bidder to acquire and operate the offshore transmission assets connecting the 1.2 GW Dogger Bank B wind farm to the UK grid. The transmission system, valued at approximately £1 billion (around €1.2 billion) by the consortium, comprises subsea and onshore cables, an offshore converter station and an onshore converter station. The consortium will operate the transmission business for 25 years after acquiring the assets and receiving an Offshore Transmission Owner (OFTO) licence from the UK energy regulator. The preferred bidder appointment is part of Ofgem’s Tender Round 11 process. Ofgem launched the tender round in February 2024 and shortlisted four bidder groups in July that year. Ofgem appointed the consortium of DTUK and Chubu as the preferred bidder on November 5. Dogger Bank B, located approximately 130 kilometers off the UK’s east coast, is the second phase of the world’s largest offshore wind farm under construction, the 3.6 GW Dogger Bank Wind Farm, owned by the consortium of SSE Renewables, Equinor, and Vårgrønn. The second phase is currently under construction, with wind turbine installation underway . The Dogger Bank B transmission system uses high-voltage direct current (HVDC) technology to transmit electricity from the offshore wind farm to the National Grid. Its offshore converter station was installed in April 2024 by Saipem’s Saipem 7000 heavy-lift vessel. DTUK is wholly owned by Global Infrastructure Partners, part of BlackRock. Following the acquisition, the company will operate eleven UK OFTO projects with a combined capacity of almost 7 GW and a total transferred asset value exceeding GBP 5.5 billion (around €6.6 billion), according to the consortium. For Chubu, the Dogger Bank B project will be its third UK offshore transmission investment, following its participation alongside DTUK in the Walney Extension and Hornsea 1 OFTO projects. The Japanese utility said it would contribute its technical expertise in transmission systems while building experience in HVDC technology and the operation and maintenance of subsea transmission assets. articles.title: Golar's New FLNG Unit to Feature Techouse Fuel-Saving Systems
articles.summary: Techouse has secured a contract from Black & Veatch to supply heat recovery steam generation (HRSG) modules for Golar LNG's fourth floating liquefied natural gas (FLNG) project, with the system expected to reduce fuel consumption by 20-25% compared…
articles.body: Golar's New FLNG Unit to Feature Techouse Fuel-Saving Systems Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 10, 2026 Illustration of Golar’s FLNG units (Credit: Golar LNG) Techouse has secured a contract from Black & Veatch to supply heat recovery steam generation (HRSG) modules for Golar LNG's fourth floating liquefied natural gas (FLNG) project, with the system expected to reduce fuel consumption by 20-25% compared with conventional gas turbine-only systems. The contract covers two HRSG modules weighing approximately 1,000 tonnes each, along with supporting systems, Techouse announced on November 10. Techouse will deliver the equipment as a subcontractor to Black & Veatch, which is responsible for the FLNG topside solutions. The HRSG technology recovers heat from the exhaust of gas turbines used to drive compressors for LNG production, generating pressurised superheated steam that can be used to produce electricity through steam turbines and supply heat to the LNG process. Engineering and procurement will be managed from Techouse's offices in Norway, while its partner Alpha ECC will manufacture the HRSG units in Vung Tau City, Vietnam. The equipment will then be shipped to Himile Heavy Industries in China for assembly into complete HRSG modules. Work on the project is starting immediately, with delivery of the modules planned by the end of 2028. Techouse will also provide installation and commissioning support. “This is a large and strategically important contract for Techouse, for an energy recovery technology that we have delivered multiple times to similar offshore projects. We look forward to supporting Black & Veatch and Golar LNG in making this project a success,” said Svein Helge Pettersen, CEO of Techouse. The company previously supplied HRSG technology for FLNG Gimi and FLNG Esperanza, but the latest award marks its first contract to deliver complete HRSG modules to Black & Veatch/Golar LNG. On October 7, 2026, Golar LNG announced an agreement to acquire the LNG carrier Grace Dahlia from NYK Line, with the vessel intended for conversion into its fourth FLNG unit. The conversion project is targeting final redelivery in 2029.

articles.title: UK offshore supply chain looks overseas for growth
articles.summary: The UK’s offshore energy supply chain is increasingly looking overseas for new business as uncertainty surrounding domestic projects threatens investment, jobs and specialist engineering capacity, according to a new industry report. Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) found that just 35% of 60 companies surveyed were...
articles.body: Europe Offshore UK offshore supply chain looks overseas for growth Bojan Lepic November 10, 2026 0 337 1 minute read OEUK OEUK The UK’s offshore energy supply chain is increasingly looking overseas for new business as uncertainty surrounding domestic projects threatens investment, jobs and specialist engineering capacity, according to a new industry report. Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) found that just 35% of 60 companies surveyed were confident about their UK business prospects over the next 12 months. Meanwhile, 80% expect more future investment and growth to come from international markets. The findings form part of OEUK’s Supply Chain Report 2026, which examines the pressures facing engineering companies, manufacturers, vessel operators, logistics providers, and other businesses supporting offshore energy developments. The trade body identified approximately £123bn ($165.5bn) of potential UK offshore energy capital investment between 2026 and 2035 but warned that many projects remain uncertain. According to the report, 95% of companies surveyed believe they could expand capacity if domestic offshore activity increased. However, without commercially viable contracts and more predictable project schedules, suppliers risk redirecting personnel, equipment and investment to countries offering greater certainty. Oil and gas remains particularly important, with nine in ten surveyed companies deriving more than 20% of their revenue from the sector. OEUK warned that offshore wind, carbon capture, and other emerging energy markets have not yet generated sufficient activity to replace traditional oil and gas work at scale. Katy Heidenreich, OEUK’s supply chain and people director, called for continued investment in domestic oil and gas alongside renewable energy developments. The organisation also urged project developers to engage contractors earlier and provide clearer procurement schedules. OEUK cautioned that losing specialist offshore capabilities now could leave the UK increasingly dependent on overseas suppliers when future energy projects move into construction. articles.body: Asia Middle East Tankers Asyad and MOL sell ageing LR2 for $63m Adis Ajdin November 10, 2026 0 596 1 minute read Michael Hatje / Marine Traffic Michael Hatje / Marine Traffic Oman’s Asyad Shipping and Japanese shipping giant Mitsui OSK Lines (MOL) have agreed to sell their jointly owned LR2 product tanker, extending the Omani owner’s campaign to cash in on ageing tonnage. The Muscat-listed company disclosed that the 2009-built Haima , held through a 50:50 joint venture with MOL, has been sold for OMR24.3m ($63.2m). The transaction is expected to generate a gain of approximately OMR19m ($49.4m) at joint venture level, with Asyad’s share amounting to OMR9.5m ($24.7m), subject to final closing adjustments and accounting treatment. The 110,077 dwt tanker has been part of the company’s fleet since construction. The buyer has not been named, and completion is expected during the second half of November. The latest disposal follows Asyad’s September agreement to sell three older tankers for a combined OMR68.44m ($178m). That package involved the 2011-built VLCCs Seeb and Samail , alongside the 2008-built MR tanker Al Amerat . The company has been recycling capital from older ships into a substantial fleet expansion programme. Its recent investments include eight MR product tanker newbuildings at HD Hyundai, all backed by five-year charter arrangements, as well as additional VLCCs at Hanwha Ocean. Asyad has said it will continue evaluating disposals of older vessels as part of its fleet renewal programme. articles.body: Europe Offshore Energean taps Njord Survey for North Sea decom work Bojan Lepic November 10, 2026 0 306 1 minute read ODE Asset Management ODE Asset Management Swedish marine survey specialist Njord Survey has secured a contract from Energean to undertake post-decommissioning seabed surveys at three gas fields in the southern North Sea. The contract covers Wenlock, Garrow, and Kilmar, where survey work will assess the seabed following the removal of platforms and associated subsea infrastructure. Njord will carry out geophysical and environmental surveys across the former platform locations and pipeline routes, using multibeam echosounders, side-scan sonar, underwater cameras and environmental sampling equipment. The findings will be compared with earlier surveys to assess the impact of decommissioning activities and support Energean’s final reporting to UK regulators. Njord plans to deploy its own survey vessels, equipment and personnel for the work. Financial details and the execution schedule were not disclosed. Energean has already made substantial progress with its decommissioning programme in the region. In September, the company confirmed that the topsides and jackets at Garrow and Kilmar had been removed during a campaign involving Petrodec’s OBNA jackup vessel. The operation involved approximately 3,373 tonnes of offshore infrastructure, while removal of the Wenlock platform was scheduled for October. Garrow and Kilmar are located within the Southern North Sea Special Area of Conservation, making environmental monitoring an important part of the close-out process.
